speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like at this time to bring to the attention of the house a question of privilege affecting the independence of my position as a member of parliament. I think you and the house should be immediately advised that it has been suggested that I use my influence as a member of the house in a most improper way, and that I have been threatened that failure to do so would bring reprisals by way of personal attacks against me in the house.
I have to advise that I was approached yesterday evening in connection with certain questions which have been raised in the house during recent days affecting my personal position. A highly respected member of the press gallery, Mr. W. A. Wilson, chief of the Montreal Star parliamentary press bureau, advised me that he had been requested by Mr. Pascal Hayes, the Progressive Conservative candidate in the Montreal Notre Dame de Grace riding in the April 8 federal election, and presently employed I am advised in the office of the Leader of the Opposition, to convey to me the following message. Mr. Hayes indicated that if I would undertake to have quashed a conviction for common
assault which is now outstanding against him and which is presently under appeal in the Quebec courts, he would cause certain members of the opposition to cease making any further personal attacks or imputations against me in this house, and that there would be no further attacks from the Progressive Conservative party in this house. If I failed to take this action, I was given to understand that these attacks would be continued and that other Progressive Conservative members would be organized to take part. I was advised also that the Conservative members of the banking and commerce committee would walk out of the meeting tomorrow morning.
With respect to Mr. Hayes' conviction, I was advised to use any means possible to have the charge dropped or withdrawn or the conviction quashed, so as to leave his record completely clean. It was further suggested particularly that I should arrange for a key witness in the prosecution to say that it was not Mr. Hayes who had struck her but, in fact, was a certain Mr. Cameron who also was implicated in the case, who gave testimony at the original trial, and who was one of Mr. Hayes' election organizers. It was stated that I should see that Mr. Hayes came out of the case "clean".
As you can readily recognize, this involves a very serious question with possible far reaching effects. I considered it to be my duty as a member of this house and a citizen of this country to lay this matter before you and this house at the very first opportunity.

[Editor's note: statement referred to above is as follows:]
Earlier this year the Voice of Women presented me with a brief entitled "Fall-out monitoring in Canada." It did not seem to be appropriate for me to comment on such a complex matter before it was thoroughly reviewed. This brief has now been reviewed by competent scientific officers and I also referred it to the dominion council of health. The dominion council of health is the senior advisory committee to the department and all of the provinces are represented on it by their deputy ministers of health or chief medical officers, as the case may be. The council reviewed the brief and prepared the following statement on October 25, 1963.
Ionizing radiation, its effect on health and the development of radiation protection services are matters which receive the regular and close attention of council. The present meeting was no exception and the dominion council of health received and discussed in detail the report of the radiation protection division of the Department of National Health and Welfare. In addition it dealt with the matters raised in the brief from the Voice of Women entitled "Fall-out monitoring in Canada", which had been referred to council by the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Council recorded the following views which are pertinent to the points brought out in this brief.
Detection of fall-out is only one of five interrelated factors which must be considered in assessing the total effects of this source of ionizing radiation on health. The dominion council of health, after full consideration of all information available, found no indication for the implementation of additional detection measures recommended in the brief submitted by the Voice of Women nor does the dominion council of health consider that there is justification, at the present time for "the installation of milk decontamination equipment by the dairy industry". Fall-out must be kept in proper perspective with other forms of radiation exposure.
The dominion council of health is satisfied that the present radiation protection program of the department and plans for its further development are fully adequate to meet the needs of this country.
The dominion council of health supports the proposal of the Department of National Health and Welfare for the establishment of an expert committee on all aspects of radiation protection and furthermore recommends that the brief submitted by the Voice of Women be studied and reported upon by this committee.
I concur in this statement, and I would like to assure the members of this house that the department has been in regular consultation with experts in Canada and in other countries on matters of radiation protection since the program was set up in 1950. Every effort has been made to develop and maintain a highly competent service and at the same time to

Hon. members will recall that the Customs Tariff contains an item, 1201, which prohibits the importation of "books, printed paper, drawings, paintings, prints, photographs or representations of any kind of a treasonable or seditious, or of an immoral or indecent character".
I should explain that the detention of a publication by customs should not be interpreted as prohibition of the publication, since any customs officer is duty bound to detain any work which in his judgment is immoral or indecent and submit it to the department for examination and a ruling as to its classification in the light of item 1201.

I want to make a few comments on the method of designation of areas, which provides that they must have less than 50 per cent of the national average employment over eight years, and have high summer unemployment. This is a very discriminatory method of designating areas, because there are many tourist areas which have high summer employment but still suffer severely from a high rate of winter unemployment.
I would like to ask the minister what research, if any, has been made with regard to the designated areas. I am sure some of them have been areas of full employment in the past, and what assurance is there that after the expenditure of hundreds of thousands of taxpayers' dollars, the same conditions will not exist which drove industry out of those areas previously? In other words, has any investigation been made into whether the climate in those areas is favourable or unfavourable for industrialization? Has any investigation been made into water and sewerage facilities, and the general conditions existing? Has it been determined whether an industry which goes into a particular area is likely to flourish in that area?
It is a strange situation that the designated areas in Ontario are ones which are represented by cabinet ministers. I could name some of them, but at the moment my strong objection is to the method of designation. To my mind it contravenes dominion-provincial relations and dominion-provincial-municipal relations. Surely the person on the ground, who lives in an area, collects taxes, and observes it over the years, knows whether it is an area that wants help.
As far as I can see, this government is staking a knowledge of statistics against the
Income Tax Act
knowledge of people. To my mind that is altogether wrong, and for these reasons I cannot support this bill.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to make a few remarks with regard to Bill C-95. We are now discussing clause 16, which says:
This new section provides a 36 months exemption from tax for income tax from a new manufacturing or processing business in a designated area. This clause implements paragraph 2 of the income tax resolution which reads as follows-
I want to draw the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) to this matter. I would like to defend small business: there are quite a number of small industries throughout Canada, and quite a few in the province of Quebec, which can barely operate. Many of those small industries would need some sort of help, but, according to this clause, only new industries will benefit from those income tax exemptions.
With regard to industries which have been operating for some time, I believe it will be rather difficult to have them move to other areas. For instance, industries that are in centralized areas, like Quebec, Montreal, or Sherbrooke, are not likely to go and settle in some other area without proper means of transportation, or where transportation is much more costly and markets inadequate. Let us, for instance, take an industry in the city of Montreal: according to statistics, it can sell almost 25 per cent of its production locally; but, if that industry settles elsewhere, it will lose this advantage of selling 25 per cent of its production locally, without having to pay for transportation.
And the larger centres offer many other advantages which do not exist elsewhere. In a centre like Montreal-to take that city again as an example-where there is an abundance of specialized labour, industry does not find it too difficult to obtain what it needs in that field.
On the other hand, while there is plenty of manpower in remote centres, there is no skilled labour force. The industry which will set up in those centres will have to train and organize a new manpower. Small industries have much difficulty in getting established and in maintaining their development, because of the many problems which the larger centralized industries do not have.
For instance, as regards the manpower problem, the small industry must organize it itself and train the young people of the area. There is practically no skilled labour in those areas. So, the small industry must train the workers.
According to the statistics I have here, the small industry must train some ten

Income Tax Act
people before it can keep one skilled worker who will be able to do the job. The small industry must train several persons because once they know their trade, there are always some who will go to work in the larger centres where skilled labour is in great demand and better paid. So, the small industry has to train about ten people in order to keep at least one trained worker, which means that its costs are that much higher and its profits, that much lower.
With regard to the financing of small industries in remote centres, where can they find the help they need? In the first place, the various governments, federal, provincial, municipal, the school boards, the church councils collect taxes and sell debentures on a year round basis. The governments undertake campaigns to sell debentures, and consequently all the money goes to them.
The federal government, for instance, sells a lot of debentures; the provincial governments, the school boards and the municipalities do the same. In the meantime, the small industries also try to sell debentures to raise capital but they get only what is left. Sometimes they are unable to find the money needed for expansion, which means they have to spend years barely managing to survive.
I know personally several small industries, and am apprised of the difficulties they are up against, in that field. Some of them have been operating their plants or their businesses for ten or 15 years practically without profit. I even know industries which have been in operation for ten years, and have suffered yearly losses of $10,000, $15,000 or $20,000, those losses being made good by the income of some more profitable ventures. On the eleventh year, there is profit at last. But, then it has to pay income tax, whereas it should be granted an exemption to make up for the losses of the previous years.
Now, that is the matter upon which I call the attention of the Minister of Finance. I feel that it would be a good thing to grant small industries the same tax exemption the new industries are getting under the policy the Minister of Finance has set out in Bill C-95.
These small industries, which can barely make ends meet, cannot find the capital they need, except through banks which lend at an interest rate of about 10 per cent. However, some municipalities have begun to help out industry.
There is the industrial development bank whose function we all know. But an industry must have been in operation for three years and earned profits. If an industry cannot meet those conditions, the industrial development bank is not interested.

As the small industry cannot get a loan from the industrial development bank, nor from other sources, because all the money goes for the purchase of all sorts of debentures issued by the federal, provincial and municipal governments, I believe that it is in real need of tangible assistance in order to develop.
The expansion and development of small industries, I believe, would be less expensive than to establish new ones because, as I said before, new industries are not interested in settling in new areas which are located far from the larger centres. Furthermore, only the local folks, who like to live there, who have their relatives there, would agree to remain there and work for those industries.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, on account of all the factors involved, the Minister of Finance will have to show more concern for the problems of the small industry, because its requirements are basic. It is essential to help small industries, if we are to provide for the development of the whole country.
It is recognized that industry is the basis of capital, the basis of social economy. It is recognized that industry puts into circulation the money of the employees, to provide a living for the professionals, who live from workers' salary. The professionals live on the money they draw from those who earn it in industry. In general, almost all the professionals live on what the worker gives them. In turn, the worker takes his money in industry. However it is to industry that the less attention is paid. Our attention should be directed towards the smaller industries which will grow one day.
A three years or 36 months tax exemption is not so much to give assistance to industry. To really help industry, the larger industries should be encouraged to move to the various centres, and the government should do something entirely different, for instance, pay 50 per cent of the cost of the removal and of the construction of plants. The government should pay grants on transportation. Otherwise, industry will not be encouraged to resettle, and the government will then have to do something else.
I therefore do not believe that the amendment to Bill C-95 brought forward by the Minister of Finance will be of great help to the people and to Canada. I am of the opinion that the best service the minister could render would be to take an already existing industry and set it on its feet again, to see to it that it can at least survive, by granting it the tax exemption granted new industries.
That is why, Mr. Chairman, I have an amendment to submit to the Minister of Finance so that he may clarify his bill as

much as possible. I know that the minister will look into the problem and will try to find solutions.
The amendment which I propose reads as follows:
I move, seconded by Mr. L. P. Antoine Belanger, that section 16 of the bill be amended by adding section 16 A which reads as follows:
This section will also apply to small industries already set up in the said designated areas, in addition to industries which will improve their plants or buy new equipment.
This is the amendment which I submit to the house, Mr. Chairman.

speechtext:

Before we proceed any further I would like to note that the other day the hon. member for Renfrew South indicated in an article that there was not enough polarization of debate and the people of Canada did not see enough difference in principle between the two major parties. What I wish to underline this afternoon is that in our discussion of designated areas there is a definite difference in principle regarding our approaches to this problem.
One of the main principles of the party I support in this house goes back to the time of Burke when the idea of local self-agency was promoted. It simply means that municipalities often know what is best for themselves and how best to govern their own affairs. This is a major difference in approach as between the two major parties.
We consulted the municipalities:	You
designated without consultation. When we brought in the notion of surplus manpower areas we never went forward unless the municipalities were consulted in advance, and this is a principle that is written right into the heart of my party's approach. A treasury bench, one third of which is made up of exsenior bureaucrats, has adopted this attitude of designation without consultation, and that is what we are fighting against this afternoon.
I fully realize that the government of the day has a great responsibility in the field of stimulating the economy and employment, but I ask members of the government, have you not learned your lesson yet? Have you not learned your lesson that your whole economic problem has floundered because of lack of consultation? You never consulted the provinces in relation to your pension scheme or in relation to the municipal loans fund question. Lack of consultation keynotes the whole reason why the government is floundering in relation to its economic program; and in relation to the first area it designated I ask, is not the proof of the pudding in the making?

I do not want to underrate the importance of statistics. Of course in a plan such as the government has in mind, statistics and centralized control here in Ottawa, play an important part in determinations before designating an area; but what we would like to know either from the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Industry, or the Minister of Labour, is whether in future the municipalities are going to be consulted before they are designated. If the hon. member for Renfrew South really wants polarization in debate, this notion of consultation is one that separates the two major parties in the house.
The party I support was the party which fathered confederation. Today we are fathering, again and again, this notion of co-operative federalism. Through our ARDA program and in the field of natural resources we went forward in good will, in co-operation and in a spirit of consultation with the provinces. We are the ones who have pioneered this whole area of co-operative federalism. Hon. members opposite talked about co-operative federalism in their speech from the throne, but their whole performance since then has been keynoted by a retreat from that spirit of cooperative federalism. Unless they accept our warning today, and assure us they will consult the municipalities in future before designating areas, then in a very short time we shall witness in this house-and mark my words-another retreat.
In a by-election in a constituency across the water somebody recently made the remark-and I think the remark was based on Conservative principles-that Westminster does not necessarily know what is good for Scotland. I think, underlining Conservative principle in this house, and especially in a nation with a large land area and sparse-population, that Ottawa, no matter how wise the ex-bureaucrats are, does not always know what is best for the municipalities.
If you really believe in centralization across there, and I believe you do-you are the centralizers-you need have no fears by simply extending to municipalities, local governments and provinces the courtesy of consultation, because you will not necessarily be delegating your powers away forever. Before this debate is over I hope either the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Industry, Minister of Labour, or all of them together, will assure us that this spirit of co-operative federalism, inspired and pioneered by the government I supported prior to the last election, will be put into effect. I mention our approach to ARDA and the resources field, and hon. members opposite must realize, no matter what they say or think, that municipalities are still creatures of the provinces.

In reply to the point of order I simply say I am not entering a general debate, I am talking about the specific principle of consultation, and all I ask before I take my seat is that one of the ministers concerned with this clause should guarantee to us that the courtesy of consultation will be invoked before any further areas are designated. This is hot a general debate, but I repeat that this principle separates the major parties in the house in relation to their approach to this and similar problems.

Mr. Chairman, it seems to me the government should think again and change its mind about this clause which infringes upon provincial autonomy, since municipalities are under the provinces' jurisdiction.
Now, I wonder why the government did not ask the provinces to designate the areas where unemployment and economic stagnation were more serious than elsewhere. Surely, it would have been easy and more in keeping with the autonomy of the provinces to have the provinces themselves designate those areas and submit the required recommendations to the federal government.

I fail to understand the government's attitude. We hear the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Lamontagne) speak often enough of handing back to the provinces their taxation rights. He is an advocate of the new federalism.
What does he mean by this new federalism, when certain measures are being forced upon municipalities without the provinces being consulted?
I am of the opinion that this is not the way to get better co-operation between the federal government and the provinces; on the contrary, I believe that the government's position is to ignore the provinces, and this prompts me to ask the minister a question.
Why does the government decline to ask the provinces to designate those areas? We shall know from the minister's answer what the position is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would be glad to answer the hon. member. I think that question would be more properly put to the Minister of Industry when his estimates are up for consideration.

I do not think so.

I think that the minister is afraid to answer, because he realizes that his government has made an error by refusing to ask the agreement of the provinces. In my opinion, the government is unwise in refusing to revise its attitude in that regard.

Last Friday I spoke briefly on this bill and pointed out the problems experienced by small businesses which might wish to establish a new business or a subsidiary in a designated area.
The other day I noticed in the Ottawa Journal that the Minister of Industry, addressing the Ottawa Rotary Club, said that, although the government was concerned with industry, its interests did not lie in directing it or running it but, rather, in aiding it to expand and provide employment. When one looks at this particular subclause of clause 16 he wonders who had what in mind when this provision was drawn up. I refer specifically to subclause 3. May I read it briefly and explain how I interpret it. It says:
For the purpose of this section, a person shall be deemed not to have been carrying on a business in a designated area in a fiscal period unless
(a) throughout the fiscal period the aggregate of the capital cost of all machinery, equipment (other than delivery equipment) and buildings situated in the designated area that were owned by the person-
Subclause A deals with owned machinery, and it goes on under B to deal with leased

machinery. Then it says, in line 17, that the aggregate amount must be at least 95 per cent of the aggregate of the capital cost of machinery, equipment-other than delivery equipment-and buildings wherever situated.
I would be very interested to have the minister's interpretation of what the words "wherever situated" mean. My interpretation is that the parliament of Canada cannot legislate with regard to business outside the country. Therefore, I must assume that the word "wherever" means "wherever in Canada". If this is the case, a Canadian business does not qualify because 95 per cent of the new machinery and equipment acquired must represent 95 per cent of the total assets of the company.
Let us take, as an example, a firm in the city of Ottawa which has buildings, equipment and machinery to the value of $10 million. If it wishes to establish in a designated area, whether it be in Brantford or in Blair-more it could do so, but its total assets in the city of Ottawa must represent 5 per cent of its total holdings when the new plant is built. I say that what we have really done by bringing this legislation before parliament is to open the door for foreign capital to enter this country, while closing it to our own corporations. If I am wrong in this contention, I hope the minister will explain to me, later on, what this means. My interpretation of this subclause is that it amounts to an economic boycott of Canadian industry. What is the partial solution, then? I intend to move an amendment to this clause-and I hope it will be accepted-to reduce the 95 per cent requirement. Though the fixing of any specified amount may result in a burden being imposed on certain business, a less stringent requirement would certainly be of some assistance. A partial solution, then, might be to amend the requirement from 95 per cent to 25 per cent, thus allowing smaller businesses to establish themselves, and permitting larger firms to establish subsidiaries or branch plants in the designated areas. I do not think the figure of 25 per cent is unreasonable, even if General Motors were to build a plant in one of the designated areas of the size and volume which would make the Oshawa plant representative of 5 per cent of their holdings here. I think some consideration should be given to this proposal, and I hope an explanation will be forthcoming.
I do not wish to take up any more of the time of the committee than is necessary, but I should like to summarize my views on this subject. I think the legislation as it stands precludes Canadian business from establishing subsidiary plants in designated areas, though it allows foreign companies to move
Income Tax Act
into those areas and take advantage of the income tax holiday and the accelerated capital cost allowances. This purports to be legislation to encourage businesses to establish themselves in designated areas, but it appears to me to be ill-conceived and completely unworkable. In particular, I believe line 21 of subclause 3 should be withdrawn, or reworded to eliminate its present discriminatory character. This is the line which reads "and buildings wherever situated". In view of the declared intention behind this measure, the 95 per cent requirement is unworkable and amounts to economic boycott of Canadian industry. The entire clause 16, which enacts section 71A is, in my opinion, drawn in such a way as to encourage foreign investment while at the same time denying the incentive so necessary to Canadian business.
I therefore move, seconded by my hon. friend from Regina City (Mr. More):
That clause 16 section 71A. subclause (3) be amended by substituting 25 per cent in place of 95 per cent in line 17 and by substituting 25 per cent in place of 95 per cent in line 45.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, before we vote on this question I should like to point out that the hon. member is absolutely wrong in stating that this in any way favours foreign-owned businesses moving into an area. The reason for using 95 per cent is to ensure that industries which get advantage of the generous provisions provided under this clause, depreciation allowances, and so on, are new businesses. The reason 95 per cent is used is to ensure that new machinery, equipment and new buildings are constructed by these particular businesses.

May I ask the minister one question. I pointed out the other day that I had a delegation in my office who were prepared to build a boiler manufacturing plant in the city of Brantford. By reason of the fact that new boiler manufacturing equipment in the United States costs a lot of money-in fact it is prohibitive-they were able to buy from a company in the United States who were enlarging their facilities second hand equipment at almost one tenth the cost of new. These people would be able to put 45 people to work the day they opened, but the law precludes their doing this at all. I say again that if you do not want to accept the figure of 25 per cent let us make it 50 per cent; but let us give these smaller people some kind of break.

Does the minister think that he will accomplish his purpose with this restriction in the clause?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I thought we were on the amendment, but if I may answer the question I would be glad to. The whole purpose of this section is to concentrate on new businesses. If you include a provision which would allow these businesses to bring in second hand machinery, you are going to be competing with somebody else, which is the thing we do not want to happen.

Surely where the business qualifies and meets the other requirements of the clause, taking the minister's words, what he is trying to do is to get new businesses, so surely the fact that new equipment may be necessary or may not should not make any difference. Does a new business need to have everything new? I think it is most unreasonable to say that they would have to get new equipment, that they would have to buy new equipment whether they are starting a new business or not. In other words, the cost of new equipment might preclude the starting of a new business. It seems to me most unreasonable that that should be the case. In other words, the minister says: "You are a new business, but look out, boys, we want to have no competition, or do not want you to compete with others". I do not want to use the word "ridiculous", but it is really a ridiculous assumption that this would preclude a new business from starting operations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Just in answer to that, if we went along with the suggestion made by the hon. member-and I must say I sympathize with him when he gets down to that specific case-if we did open it up like this, it would be an invitation to all sorts of businesses just to sell their present machinery to somebody else. This machinery would then become second hand and we would find we were trying to deal with something which we would not be able to handle.
I may not have pointed this out to the minister, but the equipment which these people are buying from the United States is not procurable in Canada. Cannot that sort of restriction be put on it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am sure there will be the odd case like that, but I do not think there will be very many. When this was being considered we attempted to find a broad definition which would not be subject to wide abuses, and that is why it is provided in this way.

raise the economic growth of the community.
I think that is the principle, and we are all agreed about that. Does it make any difference to the minister whether a man works on an old lathe or a new lathe? speechtext:
Some representations were
made to me about designated areas by the hon. gentleman who has just spoken. One of the things which was worrying him considerably was the prospect, of which I think we have had warning, that industries now operating in a non-designated area would merely pick up their machinery and equipment and move into a designated area, thus depriving the designated area of the advantages of such an area. The amendment calls for the substitution of 25 per cent instead of 95 per cent. The thing I am trying to figure out is how the figure of 95 per cent was picked. Following along the statement of the Minister of Industry, it seems to me there is a lot of suspicion about Canadian business, that there is a sort of bureaucratic suspicion about Canadian businessmen. Surely to goodness this would prevent any quick interchange of business. If a business is started in one place, I have yet to see where you can put it on a golf cart and walk across to the next tee or hole, as it were, and start it again in another place. You just cannot do it; it is a costly and time consuming business. So I come back to this word "suspicion", and I think this is wrong.

On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, I submit to you that basically the debate at this time should really be limited to the question of whether or not documents which have been refused by the crown can be refused for the reasons stated by the minister. I submit that if a minister comes into the house and states that by reason of the prerogative of the crown it would not be in the public interest to make documents available or alternatively, if he comes in here and says that the documents are private correspondence and the private property of some individual subject of the crown and for that reason should not be disclosed to the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm and to the world at large, hon. members are in the position of having to accept the minister's word. Therefore it would not be in order to go into the character of the documents or the type of correspondence it might

be, because for that very reason the private interests of an individual citizen would be disclosed in public, and I would submit this would be against the proper order of the house.
If I may, I should like to refer to Bouri-not's Parliamentary Procedure, fourth edition, page 249, where I find the following:
Occasions may arise when the government will feel constrained to refuse certain papers on the ground that their production would be inconvenient or injurious to the public interests. A high authority writes on this point: "Considerations of public policy and a due regard to the interests of the state, occasionally demand that information sought for by members of the legislature should be withheld, at the discretion and upon the general responsibility of ministers."

The motion is one calling on the government to produce the documents referred to in the motion. The question in issue is whether or not they should be produced. It would be relevant to debate whether or not the grounds of objection were sufficient but in my view it would not be relevant to debate what the government should be doing about the breadth of international waters. I feel that this is the very essence of democratic principles. As a representative of the people and in keeping with democratic principles, I have a right to obtain those papers even though the letters are marked "Personal" or "Confidential".
The minister refuses to table those letters. I actually know that correspondence was exchanged between Mr. Roland Comtois and officials of the Department of Public Works. Moreover, if there had been correspondence marked "personal and confidential" exchanged between Mr. Comtois and the Minister of Public Works, which correspondence would have been filed in the personal records of the Minister of Public Works, I maintain that I should not be compelled to table it.

speechtext: At that rate, any correspondence addressed to a minister by a former candidate or by a man who would like to extend his patronage to a riding could be stamped "personal and confidential" and would become untouchable since we could not ask to have it produced. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if I understand the case in point now submitted by the member for Lapointe, it deals with letters bearing the words "personal and confidential" and addressed to the minister, which would be placed in the personal file of the minister in his office or in his department; I must say that according to parliamentary experts and in compliance with the tradition followed down through the years, we should not be obliged, I do not say "not to table", but we should not be obliged to table that correspondence.

I have here May's book and at page 273 of the sixteenth edition, he comments as follows:

The papers and correspondence sought from government departments should be of a public and official character and not private or confidential.

That author clearly said that documents between an individual and the department, or the officials of a department, can very well be tabled, but that it is different for a private and confidential document.
Mr. Speaker, I think my hon. friend from Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm who was a member of a government which, during six years, consistently agreed to that recognized principle does not expect that I can be obliged to table personal and confidential documents which might be in my personal file. The hon. member for Lapointe has enough imagination to go far beyond the matter with which we are dealing at the moment; but I feel quite sure that there must be in a minister's files some private file, with correspondence of a personal and confidential nature, that the minister should not be compelled to produce.
If the hon. members would think matters over, they might see things in that light.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in making this, my first attempt, at explaining the estimates of the department and defending my management, I do so with some diffidence for a variety of causes. In the first place, I have been the minister of the department for only six months, and the estimates we are discussing tonight are estimates with which I had nothing to do. Indeed, most of them have already been spent. I think most hon. members will agree that the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources probably has a wider range of responsibilities than any other government department. I have limitations as to those things I can usefully say at this stage. However, I shall be happy later to discuss specific programs and areas of work when the relevant votes come before the house.

Supply-Northern Affairs
I think hon. members are aware of the tremendous diffusion of the department. There is the administration of northern Canada, with all that that entails in the development of both human and material resources; research into water resources and advice on the management of water supply; the great national parks of Canada; and then, the cradle of our history which we call national historic sites and monuments; the management of wildlife in Canada, the national museum and a number of other related resource topics that all come within this department.
Last summer during the recess, Mr. Chairman, it was my good fortune to make an extensive tour of northern Canada. I must take note at this time that the hon. member for Northwest Territories did not like my proceeding to northern Canada. I can only assure him that I am going to do it again and again in the future. Like most hon. members, I had not previously had the opportunity of seeing northern Canada. I rather doubt if any great number of members in this house have been in what we call northern Canada, including the Arctic. Some of them have. I think they will agree with me that when you first see that country you change your predetermined concepts concerning it.
I do not propose to repeat a lot of platitudes about the north

and there have been platitudes. The north has subsisted, in part, upon reputation. There has been the romance of the north. I have nothing against romanticism. As a matter of fact I think the red shadow, for a period of a generation, kept alive a great stretch of sandy desert in north Africa. The stories that are coming out of our north country are giving a tremendous reputation to this part of the country, to the gratification of those who want to see it as a tourist paradise. I do not object in any way to the considerable writings about northern Canada at the present time. But it is a very difficult thing to understand any part of the country through second hand information.
The immediate problem which has been recognized by successive governments, and this is not a partisan matter, is how to make a reality of the human and material potential that is existing there. I think my predecessor in this post would agree with me that the fundamental problem of the north is economic. This is not entirely a problem for governments, though certainly they have a role to play in co-operation with soundly based private enterprise. What can be done to help broaden the economic base of the region so it can provide a satisfactory standard of living for its growing population and contribute
[Mr. Laing.l
to the economy as a whole? This is the question with which we are confronted in dealing with northern Canada. Let there be no mistake that the economic base must be broadened, or any doubt that the population is growing very quickly.
Historically, we would say that the important residents of the north, the Eskimo population, were able to depend on hunting and fishing to maintain their traditional way of living. These traditions are gone and will not return. With southern medicine and medical care, the population in most areas has grown far beyond the capacity of the local resources of game and fish to support it. The people in the south are no longer prepared to see disease and starvation hold the northern population to the limits set by the local food supply. The Eskimo people themselves have become aware of our southern comforts and conveniences and are no longer prepared to live in the way their forefathers did.
I found it very significant on my northern trip that virtually all the Eskimos with whom I spoke accorded first priority to the education of their children. At this point I should like to say that I sincerely hope, indeed I know, that every member of this house is prepared to take the stand that there are no longer any generically inferior people anywhere. This applies with a special emphasis to our northern people. I found the Eskimo people, pushed off on ice and rock, extremely able people. Those who have been given some education in our schools are shortly going to present themselves to Canadians, probably in other parts of Canada, as well informed, well integrated, well balanced people who want to take part in the future of this Canada, which is theirs as much as ours. This means education in the ways and techniques of the south, in schools based essentially on a southern pattern modified to meet northern needs.
As hon. members know, the schools are there. Most northern children, of whatever racial origin, can now go to school; and within about five years this opportunity will be open to all of them. Well qualified students will soon be graduating in substantial numbers and will be looking for work. However the jobs are not there now, and they will have to be provided. The economic base must expand.
With particular reference to the western Arctic, beginning at what I would describe as Hay River and going up the Mackenzie river, I find great promise at the present time. The projected railway to Hay River, with its branch line to Pine Point, is going to have the effect of moving freight up to about

latitude 62. At Hay River, where a devastating flood took place in May of this year, the town has recovered, and in the shipping period from about June 8 until October 25 freight going up the Mackenzie rose 50 per cent over last year.
There is abundant evidence that mining companies, and resource companies, are going into the area, staking out properties, finding new minerals, and developing new mines. I want to pay my compliment to those companies, some of them giant Canadian companies, that are putting their money into an area where risk capital is needed. The tremendous mine at Pine Point, where investment is under way totalling $30 million, with a townsite that will be capable in the next four or five years of supporting 2,000 people, is one of the bright spots in Canada. Further north than that United Keno Hill, and other mines such as Giant Yellowknife, are doing exceptionally well, and by their actions are persuading an increasing amount of risk capital to go into the north country. On the western side of the Arctic, then particularly in the Mackenzie area, the outlook is extremely good.
In order to achieve these objectives, however, government must be as efficient as possible, and must reflect closely the needs of the area served. In my judgment, and I know my predecessor in the former administration agrees, this means that administration as far as possible be decentralized to the north.
The need to get government closer to the people most immediately concerned has been recognized in the bills respecting Mackenzie and Nunassiaq territories which are now awaiting second reading in this house. It is not my purpose at the moment, nor would it be in order, to discuss these bills. I would, however, like to underline the very great importance of giving them prompt and sympathetic consideration.
This urgency arises partly from the fact that the bills envisage the establishment of the new territories on April 1, 1964. This provides very little time for the federal and territorial governments and the Northwest Territories council to make the final arrangements which must await passage of the bills. A more immediate source of urgency arises from the fact that the life of the present Northwest Territories council will expire this month, on November 21 to be exact.
If the Mackenzie bill is not passed, the territories will be left without a legislature, and in that part of the world it is desirable for obvious reasons to avoid a winter election if possible. If these bills had not been before the house, an election would have been called probably for September last. As things have
Supply-Northern Affairs worked out, the territories will be without a legislature until an election can be held, or until the Mackenzie bill goes through.
This may not seem a serious matter, since the territorial council normally meets for only three or four weeks a year. However, the next meeting is scheduled for January when the annual territorial estimates will come up for consideration. The territorial council has the same authority over estimates as this house, although there is a difference in practice. Unlike our parliament, the territorial council normally considers its government's estimates before the beginning of the fiscal year to which they refer. In short, if there is no council meeting in January there will be no money available in the normal course for territorial expenditures in April.
Hon. members will be aware of the quick action of the council in passing legislation needed following the flooding of last spring. Let me say the time has now arrived when it is in the interests of the people there that they have more government on the ground and less government from Ottawa. I think the people who are there and are developing that country, are exercising and enjoying a greater confidence in their own ability to stay there and to prosper, and it behoves this parliament to extend to them as rapidly as we can further major conduct in control of their affairs at site.
As indicated earlier, Mr. Speaker, northern administration is not a partisan matter. The federal government first took an active interest in northern development during a Liberal regime. The succeeding Conservative government, to their credit, carried on and expanded these programs, and added to them to meet changing conditions. The present government does not foresee a radical departure from the broad lines established earlier, although of course conditions are not static and policies must be flexible to support them.
My predecessors used the word "vision" to describe their attitude to northern development. They have a certain moral copyright on that word, if not on the ideas that it represents. I would describe our approach to northern policy as one of imaginative realism, and I want to be realistic in respect of the north, as I am sure the people who live there also want to be.
At the present time it is an enormous deficit area. We are putting somewhere between $40 million and $50 million a year, in moneys collected from taxpayers in southern Canada, into the north country, and those people who live in the north country should not be ashamed of those circumstances, because this is the history of pioneer areas in all parts of Canada. As Canada moved west

Supply-Northern Affairs the same situation existed then, but we want as early as we possibly can, as do the people who live there, to see that they be selfsupporting, and it would seem to me to be the responsibility of the government here to adopt things and do acts in respect of assisting private enterprise to go in there, build up that country, employ people, and ultimately stand on their own feet. That is going to be our policy.
Whatever word is used, I think we would all agree that the north is an important part of the country that has been neglected for most of our history and that now deserves the best efforts and sympathetic attention of the government of Canada. To maintain, and retain our national sovereignty, because of defence and because of the resource development, it is imperative that we give continuing and even expanding attention to that country, and I was particularly relieved to note the vast new interest that is obvious in most of the Arctic, and particularly in the western Arctic, by people with private investment capital.
Now I want to deal with one or two other matters. I am quite certain my predecessor will agree with me that we have in our 19 national parks a very fine representation of the original Canada in its wilderness state, that we have preserved our national parks well, that we want to continue them for the enjoyment of the people of Canada, but at the same time we realize they have come to have a commercial aspect to the extent that they are one of the great magnets drawing an increasing number of people from other parts of the world, to visit Canada and spend their money here.
Due to the improvement of a considerable network of roads in Canada, and particularly with the imminent finalization of the trans-Canada highway, we seem to have repatriated a great amount of Canadian traffic that formerly used highways in the United States. I am aware that assisting in the repatriation has been the 92 cents condition of the Canadian dollar, but it must be admitted that our great national parks system is one of those tremendous magnets which are drawing a greater number of visitors to Canada annually, and that situation in turn is one of the bright spots in our balance of payments situation. I believe in recent years we have turned a deficit of $250 million annually into a favourable balance of some $50 million.
Historically our parks were set aside to be wilderness areas. This was the original concept, it is still the concept, and the traditionalist today who wants to go into a national park would prefer to find very few people there beside himself. He wants the great outdoors, but the traditionalist is being


confronted by hard facts at this time. A generation ago most of those who visited our national parks, particularly those in the western parks system were relatively wealthy Canadians or very wealthy Americans who came by rail bringing their families with them, and who stayed in the great hotels- hotels which provided all the services needed. During the time of their holiday in Canada they spent a considerable amount of money.
All this has changed, and the automobile has changed it. The crowds today are on rubber tires and they are really crowds. Because of statutory holidays with pay, because of a good and always improving roads system, because of the fact that cars are owned by almost everyone, most Canadian families are today throwing the kids in the back of the car and saying: "Let us see Canada; let us go to the national parks". For one reason or another, in the case of our western parks, when they get on the highway they say: "We shall drive right through to Banff", or "We shall drive right through to Jasper". I am certain my predecessor is aware of the situation. We face a crisis in our national parks. It is a crisis of plenty, not one of paucity; thank goodness for that. But here is a situation where the traditionalist is in conflict with the situation as it exists. We are faced with the necessity of providing a new type of service in our parks for these people who come in on rubber tires.
I think it is a splendid thing that the ordinary Canadian can take his family to the national parks. But, as I have indicated, we must provide as far as we can the type of service he demands. These visitors want tenting facilities; they want a place to park the trailer and they want the kind of service which makes allowance for the fact that a considerable proportion of the money allocated for the holiday is already allocated to the gas tank. We have this situation to meet. We must meet it, and at the same time retain as far as we possibly can the traditional outlook toward our national parks. That is not going to be easy. As I have said, we have undertaken to divide the administration of the parks system. We are setting up at once a station for western Canada located at Calgary, a station for central Canada at Cornwall and a station at Sydney, Nova Scotia, for eastern Canada. So hon. members will see we are decentralizing the administration. When an organization does a substantial part of its business in two months of the year it has to make decisions quickly; it is not always practicable to wire to Ottawa and wait for a reply. We are putting responsibility for purchasing and for making decisions upon

those divisional officials who will be responsible in those areas. We found last summer, particularly in the case of the western parks where a tremendous increase in visitors was experienced, that it was very difficult to take decisions in time to relieve the congested situation-a situation which was really something to behold. In Banff last year we had over a million visitors and in our parks across Canada we experienced a 24 per cent increase compared with the previous year. This was not foreseen by the department or by myself, and I am certain my predecessor would agree that an increase of such magnitude presents a startling situation. This demand for tenting facilities and parking space for trailers should not be regarded as short term in its nature. I think we must realize it is here to stay and we must make preparations to meet it.
Before I close I should like to say something about one or two of the other aspects of the work of this department. We Canadians often console our frustration over the problems of the day by reflecting that our land is a rich land, that its waters and rocks, its woods and its soils are an estate that provides a solid basis for our sovereign existence. We are not wrong in laying claim to bountiful natural resources, but we have heavier blinkers than those of the legendary Seraphim if we believe that simply having is enjoying. Our resources exist, but they are often hidden by more than physical barriers. Ignorance as to location and development techniques, well meaning parochialism as to the use of benefits, are two of the major problem areas, common of course to all states but of particular concern to resource management in a country where the interests of many governments are involved.
As in the days of the "voyageurs", although now for different reasons, waterways speak with a loud voice to dictate where the country may grow. Water is basic to human civilization; its purity and availability are taken for granted. We have come to feel this way precisely because of the scientific research which in past years has very unobtrusively supported the tapping of fairly extensive supplies. The drain grows day by day, uses multiply, the countryside is remodelled and so century old water patterns are disrupted. In the fact of this dilemma, antiquated water knowledge cannot be tolerated and for this reason I am proud of the team of water resource professional and technical people which has been built up in my department.
Their professional work falls under three headings:	(1) hydrometric measurements;
(2) sediment surveys and (3) studies of special current interest to the federal government. The hydrometric work relies on 1,750 stations through the country, 100 of which were
Supply-Northern Affairs established during the current year. The sediment work is relatively new-it is in its third year-but its value has proven itself. Indeed the life of costly reservoir works and navigation facilities cannot be divorced from the evolutionary processes that are constantly affecting any stream. Our sediment studies are bearing down on this area of ignorance. But pride in what is being done must not delude us into believing that all the answers to the problems of water usages in a complex society will be available without a constant vigilance to keep our research on top of the facts. It seems inevitable that our activity and our expenditure in this area will increase.
As I have mentioned, the department also conducts special studies in connection with current water development interest. In this connection I should like to make a passing reference to the Columbia river. I should like to say, parenthetically, that our involvement in the Columbia development project was, and is, under this heading of special studies. Extensive studies have, indeed, been undertaken by the department on this topic but since the current negotiations relative to the treaty are the concern of my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, I would suggest that discussion of this matter may be more appropriate during the consideration of his estimates. These special studies inevitably lead to the question of the respective roles to be played by the federal and provincial governments not only in the realm of water but in the wider relationship of natural resources.
At this stage, let me say I think our government has done all in its power to make the writing of a treaty in respect of Columbia water with the United States a practical thing as well as a valuable thing to Canada. While it is true that questions on the treaty itself must be directed to my colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs, I do take pride in the fact that the technical men from my department have constantly supplied our negotiators with all the relevant facts necessary to the determination of a treaty which will be of benefit to Canada if and when it can be reached.
Current literature abounds in stressing the need for a multiple-use approach to any hydro development. This approach is the threshold to the concept of thinking in terms of regional economic units, and by the same token opens the way to a field of inter-government cooperative possibilities, as well as pitfalls. To co-operate with purpose on major resource projects, not only entails investing a gigantic share of the national wealth we of this age legitimately feel is a heritage to be handed to our children, but also requires sound technical knowledge. There must be no hesitancy in

Supply-Northern Affairs providing the professional machinery to keep all those who have an interest in Canada's resources technically well informed. But this is not all that is required. Co-operation is paramount.
True co-operation depends on a spirit of trust and optimism. I can think of no better area where this can be fostered than the area of resource management. And for this reason I am particularly happy about the growth of a child, born a few years ago though conceived much earlier, and rapidly becoming a firm institution of modern federalism. Indeed the resource ministers council is now a living fact and there is no doubt in my mind that the meeting of minds that it will give rise to, will be a solution source for Canadian resource problems. It will also make the often bandied about word, "dialogue", a working concept. I am confident that under its dynamic chairman, the Hon. Rene Levesque, the council will do much more than its terms of reference may indicate.
At this stage I should like to repeat what I said yesterday to a group of people interested in our natural resources. I said the position taken by the federal government had to be an extremely cautious one. I have tremendous hope and great confidence that when the provinces, through the resource ministers council, discuss resources beyond the confines of the individual provinces concerned, remembering always that though it is the responsibility of the province to develop the resources within its own borders it is possible to develop those resources in such a manner as to do harm to its neighbours, a stage will have been reached which could result in economic achievements of great value to all Canada. As far as the federal government is concerned we shall attempt to act as catalysts, but I think the government of Canada should stand ready at all times to assist the provinces as they discuss their resource possibilities among themselves, in any way possible, financial and otherwise.
I wish to say in closing that had I been consulted by the Prime Minister with respect to any department that I might have wished for, after six months of experience of the work of this extremely varied department, I would have chosen the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. There is a tremendous challenge in it because we are dealing with resources, not only of material but resources of people as well. I can only say I shall endeavour to make a study of all branches of the department to do the best I can to use the fund voted to this department by this parliament, and to bring along and extend the borders of Canada; because we are dealing principally in this department with the only great remaining

frontier of Canada. It is extremely promising at the present time. It still has its problems, but the outlook is extremely bright. When I found the great mine at latitude 62, when I went on my trip to latitude 75, which I think is about 890 or 900 miles from the North Pole, to find them drilling for oil in an area where the geologists say the geology is such that oil must be there, and that when they find it it is going to be another Arabia-these are the terms being used-then I think there is tremendous hope for the north country. There are very few people in it at the present time, and in my view it is not a country which will support a great number of people. But it will support more than are there are the present time, and I am quite certain that the extended pursuit and search for resources is going to end in success. I am quite certain that these social capital advances we are making to the north country will in time be repaid, and if the pursuit goes on at the present rate I think they will be returned relatively early.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on occasions of this kind it is customary to exchange the usual courtesies, especially when a new minister is introducing his estimates for the first time. I am aware that we have had an opportunity earlier to exchange these compliments, but I do want to repeat tonight that I appreciate the remarks of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. He has stressed that what we are discussing tonight are estimates in which I had some part when I carried the responsibility for this department. I think the sincerest form of flattery-this is a well known phrase-is imitation. Because of the fact that the minister has expressed so much unanimity as to the policies and programs of the former administration, it seems to me that there will be no purpose served tonight in extending this discussion to an undue length.
I was also pleased to hear the minister refer to the fact that we have important legislation pending concerning a major forward step in northern development; that is the legislation to deal with the granting of greater political autonomy to the Northwest Territories. As he indicated, this is not the occasion to discuss these matters, but I would seize the opportunity provided by his observations to suggest that, even though there is some pressure of time by reason of the fact that there has been delay, in proceeding with this legislation we should not try to foreshorten the discussion that I am sure will arise once this legislation is introduced.
I would hope that as soon as possible we could have set up in this house a committee to which the legislation could be referred. As the minister has already indicated in his observations, so very few members in this

house have any personal knowledge of the north, and only those who have actually travelled north of 60 have an appreciation of the problems and the tremendous potential of this great, undeveloped and unexploited, area of Canada. I should think that the setting up of a suitable committee would make it possible for hon. members of this house who have the good fortune to serve on the committee to travel into the north. In this day of air transportation travel is no problem. We have the facilities, and within a few hours we can reach the farthermost points of northern Canada. I think it would make an outstanding contribution to an understanding of the problems and the potentials of the north were such a committee established. In addition to discussing the problems in detail, the committee could have the opportunity to meet with officials who are familiar with the problems; and hear some of the northerners themselves. This would be a big step forward in the understanding of this last frontier of Canadian geography.
My final remark on this point, Mr. Chairman, is to say that the reference of legislation before second reading to a committee is not without precedent. In this regard I mention one reference recorded in Hansard for May 14, 1946, where the house leader of that day, the Hon. Ian Mackenzie, referred the bill on reinstatement in civil employment to a standing committee before it reached the second reading stage. I think this step would obviate a lot of discussion which is bound to take place when this proposed legislation comes before the house, as well as provide an excellent educational experience for hon. members.
The minister has intimated that the north is still very much an unknown country. It has become much better known within recent years. When we have outstanding historians and political scientists of the day using the expression that Canada is a northern country with a northern heritage and destiny, I think that is indicative of just how far in recent years we have reached a new appreciation of this important part of Canada. This should not be new, of course, because the whole history of Canada has been that of a gradual movement into the northwest frontier. I am surprised as I travel around Canada to see how many communities there are, regardless of their location, who refer to themselves as a sort of gateway to the north. For example, Halifax regards itself as the guardian of the north, as does Fort William and Port Arthur. These cities refer to themselves as the gateway to the northwest, and they sit right on the United States boundary. But in the area north of 60 we have all the problems of geography, of climate, of distance, which
Supply-Northern Affairs have been peculiar to development in Canada right from the earliest moment of our history when Cartier, I believe it was, referred to the lush area along the St. Lawrence river as the land God must have given to Cain, as the country God had forgotten. We are a very rugged northern half of the North American continent.
When the minister referred to the deficit situation of the northern economy I was reminded of some of the statements made about another part of the Northwest Territories back in the 1880's when that part of Canada was regarded as an economic deficit area. In fact, people in responsible positions referred to the prairies as having no economic significance whatsoever. When the government of that day was building a railway through the prairies the critics said that this was a railway which would go from wigwam to wigwam and would not pay for its own oil. That was not long ago in Canadian history, a little over half a century. Now, with wheat pouring from the granaries of the prairies, from this part of the country which was a deficit economy and was not supposed to have much economic future, and with all the political pundits and fiscal experts saying that the wheat sales of the past few months and of the last couple of years are going to have a tremendous impact on the total economy of Canada, I am even a little more optimistic than is the minister. I would say that the same development could take place north of 60, once we have one of the great mineral resources brought into production. For example, the minister referred to oil. The Quirin report of three years ago exhaustively and carefully studied the oil potential. There had been a lot of romantic ideas and hazy notions about the oil bonanza that existed in the north, particularly in the Arctic islands. All these were confirmed by an outstanding oil geologist, Dr. Quirin in the Quirin report. He came up with phrases almost as ecstatic as the romanticists. When the first gusher comes in in the Northwest Territories I am sure it will have an impact on the economy much the same as in the case of the rapid growth and development of the wheat economy of the prairies in the early part of the present century.
It would appear that the new administration has accepted uncritically the policies that were enunciated and carried out over recent years by the former Conservative administration. This is a matter of satisfaction to me personally as well as to all members of the former administration. The department was organized in 1953. At that time prime minister St. Laurent used the phrase that over the
4512	HOUSE OF
Supply-Northern Affairs years Canadians had administered the northern regions in a state of absentmindedness. That situation prevailed right up to the recent historical past.

speechtext: And until today.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: What was that comment?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES

speechtext: In 1956-57 total expenditures for this department were more than $39 million and this year total expenditures will be approximately $83 million. If the size of the estimates is any criterion it indicates that some rather aggressive policies have been under way during recent years with respect to all the diverse responsibilities of this most interesting department. I am not going to enumerate, because these details are in the estimates. The program was one of national development in the best traditions of the Conservative party's national development philosophy.
