speechtext: You have ruined the whole speech.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I do not intend to go back in history and point out that the Conservative party has always been identified with the development of new frontiers. This is a matter of record and requires no debate. However, I wish the minister would speak to his colleague, the Secretary of State and house leader, because I feel he has not quite caught the vision yet. I know the problems. It is not only the backbenchers in the House of Commons who fail to understand the great potentialities of this huge area in our northland. It is also the members on the treasury benches.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Be careful.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
From time to time the Secretary of State has indicated that he is one who has not quite caught the vision or, in terms of the new phrase, imaginative realism, he is not even imaginatively realistic about the north. When speaking in the maritimes just a few months ago he referred to the maritimes as the last frontier and rather downgraded what has been taking place in northern Canada.
To refer to this matter in passing, this is a program that was carried out by my colleague, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, in the first instance and more recently it became my responsibility. I could talk about roads, airfields, mineral discoveries and the railroad to Great Slave lake. This latter project was not entirely welcomed with open arms by hon. gentlemen opposite when it was introduced in the house some three years ago. I am not going to dwell on this fact because


the minister embraces it just as enthusiastically as I and the others associated with me did, when we had the responsibility of government.
I see that my colleague from Peace River is in the house tonight. I hope he will take the opportunity afforded by the consideration of these estimates to make some remarks. If any member of the house more than any other can take credit for the launching of this realistically imaginative program it is my colleague from Peace River.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: What about the late Mr. Hardie?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The resource side of the north is most important, and I am optimistic in this regard. One comment I should like to make is that the members of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources who have been closely identified with this program over the past few years are all excellent and dedicated men. They seem to be caught up in the enthusiasm for this task of pioneering on this new frontier. I know that most of the men and women working in the department are enthusiastic and optimistic about the prospects of the north. This was the impression I always received in working closely with them.
Some reference has been made to the human resource aspect by way of an interjection by the hon. member for Kootenay West. I want to dwell on the human resource aspect of the north. While the population is not large I think one of the saddest periods of neglect in Canadian history is to be found in the long period of time it took for the government of Canada to assume responsibility and take an interest in the welfare of its northern citizens. When we remember that the residents of the eastern Arctic, for example, only received the franchise two years ago I do not think we have much to boast about with regard to our record in dealing with these Canadians-they are and always have been Canadians-north of 60, particularly in the high Arctic, in providing them with the normal amenities and services that are provided for Canadians elsewhere.
Two years ago they received the vote. They have now exercised their franchise in two federal elections. One of the reasons for the delay in granting the Eskimos the vote was the repeated argument, that they did not have the intelligence or the capacity to understand the issues that would be involved in a national election. In fact, I have even heard the phrase used-I will attribute it to no one-which is sometimes used by segregationists in the southern part of the United States, that the Eskimos would be voted rather than voting. They were given the vote

and I would say they have exercised this right with an intelligence and responsibility equal to that of Canadians in any part of Canada and perhaps with a greater degree of intelligence. I see that the hon. member for Northwest Territories agrees with me.
But there is a strange anomaly here involving a matter of great importance. The Eskimos in the eastern Arctic have the vote federally and they do not have it territorially. No wonder there is a demand for a greater degree of self-government and autonomy in the Northwest Territories. This is why it is so important that adequate time and provision be made in the house for a thorough discussion of the pending legislation. We do not want to be pressured, which seems to be the tactic that the house leader is adopting. He is going to hold up the legislation until the last moment, and then say: You must pass it because if you do not there will be no territorial government for the Northwest Territories.
I would remind hon. members opposite that the last important piece of legislation which gave greater autonomy was debated for a period of almost four years. I refer to the autonomy bill that was finally passed in 1905 and gave provincial status to the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. We do not want to be pressured on this matter, because there is a great vacuum of knowledge and hon. members must have complete freedom to discuss these important matters.
So far as human resources are concerned, the educational program has moved forward apace. I am sure the hon. member for Kootenay West agrees. There are now educational facilities for about 75 per cent of the young people of the north. There has been a tremendous increase in the past six or seven years. Then there is the welfare program. I hope that we might get some details of the housing program from the minister later on in this discussion. The Eskimo people are not primitive people. They have a complex culture. They are an intelligent people. This has been demonstrated by some of the northerners who have come to work in the department. I had an Eskimo secretary for several months, and she was one of the finest young ladies that you would wish to meet, capable in all respects. I could make reference to other northerners who have even outdistanced southern Canadians in competing in our complex society.
Those are the few remarks I wanted to make on northern affairs. The minister referred to the new concept that has emerged in recent years on national resources. I want to pay tribute to the Leader of the Opposition, the hon. member for Prince Albert, because
Supply-Northern Affairs it was his initiative, and no amount of carping criticism can ever gainsay this fact, that gave rise to the resources for tomorrow conference in 1961. It was out of that conference that this new concept emerged of wise management and multiple use of our renewable resources, as well as the new formula for resolving the problems of provincial-federal jurisdiction in this area. I know the hon. member for Kootenay West will confirm the fact that the log-rolling technique used to be used in dealing with the questions he asked in connection with conservation. The answer he invariably got was that this came under provincial jurisdiction and depended upon provincial initiative. This was no answer to the problem. The old buck-passing technique delayed action in the resources field far too long.
In 1961, after a period of very careful consultation, the federal resources minister and the ten provincial ministers meeting on a co-equal basis were able to come forth with this highly significant development, the resource ministers council with a supporting secretariat independent of the federal authority, independent of the provincial authority, and yet acting as the co-ordinating body between these two areas of administration. I recall one moment of inspiration that resolved a serious impasse. I recall that the resource ministers council was no longer willing to accept the chairmanship of the federal minister, which happened to be myself at the time. They said that the federal minister actually had no business on this council at all because the federal government had no resources. They condescended to allow him to remain on the council because of his responsibility in northern affairs where resources did come under his jurisdiction.
I know that suggestion was put forward with tongue in cheek, but the way we resolved the impasse was to conceive a rotating chairmanship. The first minister to assume this responsibility after the federal minister was the Hon. Mr. Spooner of Ontario, and now the Hon. Rene Levesque of Quebec is chairman. Then, it will be the turn of Prince Edward Island, the Hon. Mr. Rossiter, and so on through the whole resource ministers council. This is a major breakthrough in federal-provincial relations in the field of resources. It has been said in this house before that this formula might well be applied in other areas. As a matter of fact, it was applied in other areas by the former administration which practised, not only in word but also in deed, the vital policy of co-operative federalism.
Other examples were the roads to resources program; the Atlantic provinces power

Supply-Northern Affairs development, and the joint studies that are now under way on the national power grid; the Nelson river study; the use of the Canada Water Conservation Act on a co-operative basis by the three levels of government for the first time; the metro Toronto basin water development program, a multi-million dollar program which has the full support of the federal government; the upper Thames program; the Winnipeg flood way; all of these things came about because of the enthusiastic support of the idea of co-operative federalism by the former administration.
Then, of course, I should like to refer to ARDA, which is a development and a breakthrough of perhaps even more significance than the resource ministers council. If used intelligently and supported enthusiastically by all levels of government in this country, it will transform the face of our agricultural community over the next few years. There is just one point I should like to make in regard to this matter and that is the importance of a recreational parks program. This is a matter for federal-provincial co-operation. We had a discussion on this subject a few months ago. The parliamentary assistant to the minister, speaking on behalf of the department, accepted the idea of the urgent necessity for action in this recreational parks area. I only hope that the minister will be able to move forward as quickly as possible. I trust that this subject will come under discussion at the parks conference which will take place, I understand, on the 18th of this month. Here is another example of co-operative federalism that was initiated last year which, I am sure, is going to go a long way towards resolving a very critical problem that has emerged in the recreational park development area.
I could speak for a long time about parks tonight. The minister has referred to the pressure that is being felt year after year on our national parks system. I should like to add this little thought, that we did anticipate this tremendous increase in park population. We were referring to it three or four years ago. However, I would say that the current upsurge is larger than anyone could have anticipated and it arises in substantial part from the impact of the devalued dollar. This poor devalued dollar, which was supposed to lead Canada into bankruptcy, according to the critics of the policy at the time, has been one of the main contributors to the current buoyant state of the economy.
In the parks area there had been neglect for many years. Some of the things that were done in recent years were, first of all, the setting up of a planning division. Recommendations came out of the planning division

of the parks department, and the first one concerned a western supervisor because it was early realized we had to decentralize the responsibility in this area. Then, new policies began to emerge. We have had many discussions of the problems that arose in connection with preserving the wilderness. We came to the conclusion the only way this could be done was to have clearcut zoned areas with a service centre area, a fringe of semideveloped areas and then a section of the park which was retained in its pristine purity. There would be no equivocation about it at all. No amount of pressure would separate the parks from the original intent of the legislation. I trust that this zoning policy is moving apace under the leadership of the new minister.
The Oberlander report was another development. I hope the minister might later on indicate just what progress is being made in the implementation of the Oberlander report, and what progress is being made in a similar study that is proceeding in Jasper national park. Then, I wonder if there is any further information on the new national parks association which was organized in Toronto last March, under the leadership of Mr. William Baker, who had been closely identified with the resources for tomorrow conference. This national parks association, I feel, has a large role to play in the future park program.
Then, there were the representations of the Audubon society who wanted a park development program to go forward in connection with the centennial celebration. This is a program that had the sympathetic support of the former administration. I trust that it is also receiving the support of the new administration.
All of these ideas have emerged within recent years, and I was pleased to hear the minister indicate that he is carrying them forward to the best of his ability.

With regard to wild life conservation measures, the international joint committee on migratory water fowl had been meeting regularly to deal with the problem of declining population in respect to our migratory water fowl, and I trust that this work is proceeding apace. There would seem to be some indication of activity in this regard, because in my own constituency I notice where lands have been leased for a period of 20 years in order to preserve the wet land area, or potholes, to ensure proper breeding facilities for the duck population.

Finally, in addition to inter-governmental co-operation, in addition to the planning I have outlined, I would like to suggest that there is urgent need for intra-governmental co-operation. There are several departments of government that have responsibility in the renewable resources-the departments of agriculture, forestry, and fisheries, as well as national resources. I would hope that in addition to encouraging co-operation among the governments, the various federal government departments would move together on a co-ordinated basis in order to carry out the spirit of this new concept of wise management of renewable resources, and the multiple use of renewable resources. I think this is one way in which Canada can guard her national heritage.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is very interesting for me to take part in this debate, because this party has always been particularly interested in the conservation of human resources, and in the conservation and development of natural resources. I have no hesitation in saying that, from my experience in this house over a period of 18 years, with my pretty close knowledge of the internal workings of this department-and I have friends in each branch-and from my conversations with a lot of people closely connected with these subjects, the record of this department with respect to its treatment of human beings and natural resources is the worst of any department of government.
Having got that off my chest, I want to say I give the former minister, who has just taken his seat, full marks for what he did in his administration, particularly in his attempt to improve education for the natives in the north, to improve housing for them, and for his hard work in connection with the establishment of the resources for tomorrow conference and the principle of federal-provincial co-operation in that field. However, I do think that in certain respects he was too nice a person to deal effectively with some of the bureaucrats that exist in this department, some of these people whom you cannot mellow by ringing gospel bells. You have got to take a little tougher line.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: A soft answer turneth away wrath.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
My one criticism of the former minister is that he was a bit too nice.
Mr. Chairman, I notice the present minister is so interested in what I have to say that he has moved down opposite me and is listening attentively. I want to congratulate him on his appointment as minister of this department. Knowing his experience and achievements in the past, I presume he accepted this post because there are many 28902-5-288
Supply-Northern Affairs problems to meet and it represents the major challenge of his life. I am sure that is what it will be, and I wish him every success in all he undertakes.
He faces a very heavy task and, as he mentioned, this department has wider responsibilities than any other department of government. I think that is generally recognized. In fact one must realize this department is an empire within which have grown several smaller empires. This is somewhat natural owing to its historical development, how it has evolved, and the fact that a great many people in the administration of it were living in Ottawa and not in the north.
I wish the minister every success in all he undertakes to decentralize this administration. I was very pleased with what he had to say this evening, that he is hoping decentralization will occur, and that government will be handed over to the local people directly concerned as soon as possible. This is a step which has been advocated by members of this group for many years. When it was first mentioned some years ago I had a chat with one of these centralizing administrators in this department, and he simply pooh-poohed the idea that the people in the north were capable of governing themselves, and said that to think of including the Eskimos and natives in the proposition was out of all reason. I am glad this atmosphere has commenced to change, and I am pleased the minister is going to work in that direction.
There is another great need which the former minister mentioned. It is the need for more co-ordination and consultation within the department, and also between the department and other departments. You get this world famous water resources branch with its own computing machines adding up a mass of figures and getting one result, and you have the wildlife branch getting another result, with very little consultation as to the sociological effects of what they may undertake. You have one group looking at a matter purely from an economic point of view, and another group looking at it from the point of view of wildlife preservation for generations to come. There is need for a great deal more consultation within the department, and with other departments.
On a question like this members of this group take a strictly non-partisan approach. We try to be constructive, and I have some remarks to make with regard to administration generally, national parks and wildlife. Colleagues of mine will deal with other particular facets of this department later on in the debate.
As I said before, I firmly believe that for many years some of the administrators of various branches of this department have

Supply-Northern Affairs lacked vision. Some ol them, I know from personal experience, from conversations and correspondence, have had no understanding or appreciation of the need for evolution of democratic institutions under the conditions that have existed in the north in the last 50 years. They have had little concern for the improvement of the lives of human beings in those areas, and little concern for the development of resources.
I remember on one occasion when Mr. Winters was the minister for this department, that the deputy minister, without consulting the minister, gave a permit to the American Aluminum Corporation to deal with the investigations concerning water resources in the Yukon and Northwest Territories. This is the type of administrators we had. But when the minister heard of it he called Mr. Wilson from the United States, they had a dinner in Ottawa and he cancelled the permit himself. Mr. Wilson was very upset indeed, but the deputy minister went off and got himself a job in a welfare agency in the United Nations. There is a big improvement since then.
I have found in conversations, particularly in recent weeks, there is an increasing interest among members in the house in this department. Tuere is an increasing interest on the part of the informed public, those persons who concern themselves with these problems regardless of their parties. There has also been an increasing interest on the part of the press and of certain well known writers in this country. These people have all become generally critical of the policies of the senior administrators of the department.
Now I want to deal with just a few quotations from various reports to show how the department has responded to recommendations from committees, and so on. I cannot take the time of the committee at length, but in 1960 the estimates of this department were referred to the committee on mines, forests and waters. That committee had various officials of the department come before it who read nice little essays in some cases, and answered a few questions. However, in the report of the committee to the house, on Tuesday, June 28, 1960, in paragraph 4 it stated:
Water is one of Canada's most important resources. Carefully planned use of this resource is of the utmost importance not only to the present generation but to all those to come-
6.	The committee notes that the development of our nation is, to a marked extent, dependent on the orderly development of our water resources and that as our population and industry increase there is an increased need for careful planning of the use of water supplies.
[Mr. Herridge.l
7.	With the increased growth of the nation there is increased need for the type of investigations which are basic to the orderly development of water resources.
8.	Your committee, therefore, recommends that: the minister of northern affairs and national resources take the initiative in offering to the several provinces of Canada to undertake studies, in co-operation with the provinces, of multi-purpose river basin developments. This will require an expanded program of engineering and economic investigations designed to show the possibilities for the development of the water resources of this nation.
Having in mind the needs of the nation as a whole, not just of one province, I should like to ask the minister how the department has responded to that recommendation. I happen to know that some of his officials are pooh-poohing certain suggestions made with respect to the need for greater supplies of water in future in the prairie provinces, and the possibility of getting them from a very appropriate source.
Then the committee went on to make certain recommendations with respect to the power resources of this country. It said vigorous research was required to study long distance power transmission. It spoke of the necessity for establishing a national grid and for the economic use of the power resources of the nation. I should like to ask the minister if the officials of his department have carried on any studies in this field, having in mind the development of the power resources of this country in relation to the needs of Canada as a whole.
The committee dealt, also, with the important question of pollution. Paragraph 10 of the recommendations states:
Your committee recommends that the federal government accelerate investigations of pollution problems in Canada, particularly in those areas where it has legislative responsibility. In addition, at the request of the provinces, it should provide information which would be useful in establishing objectives of water quality control.
The committee then goes on to recommend certain procedures in this regard. I should like to know what has been done by the appropriate branch of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources to give effect to these recommendations on pollution control made by the committee on mines, forests and waters in 1960.
When I get an opportunity I take home one of the books containing the observations and recommendations of the royal commission on government organization, and use it as bedtime literature. Recently, I was using one of these books and I noticed a paragraph which reads:
Research In the north of Canada Is carried on by several departments and agencies of the federal government and by private organizations and individuals.

Later, it says:
While all scientific departments have some interest in the north, northern affairs and national resources has general and special interests and its responsibilities must be borne in mind in any assessment of the research roles of government departments in the north.
The report goes on to complain of overlapping of research work being done by a number of departments. Paragraph 31 of volume 4 of the report states:
Co-ordination of the multifarious northern scientific programs is in theory the responsibility of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. The advisory committee on northern development has the following terms of reference:
To advise the government on questions of policy relating to civilian and military undertakings in northern Canada and to provide for the effective co-ordination of all government activities in that area.
The report goes on to imply that this is only the case in theory. According to the report, the officials are more concerned with building up their own little spheres of influence and things of that sort. Further on, conclusions are reached.
The present system is wasteful of money and personnel and does little to ensure that necessary research is being carried out. Certain conclusions are evident. Co-ordination of scientific work in the north and the determination of priority should be the concern of the proposed central scientific bureau.
The report goes on to deal with the way in which research might be carried on. Then the commissioner recommends, in paragraph 46:
1.	That the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources meet its northern research needs by contracting with other federal departments or private groups, and
2.	That facilities and services for research in the north be provided by the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources.
There we find a definite criticism of the efficiency of the department in this respect. I should like to know what the department has done to remedy this situation since the report of the royal commission was tabled in this house.
Then, again, as will be found on page 162 of volume 3, the commissioner recommends with respect to the administration of the department of northern affairs:
That the operation of the northern school system be transferred as rapidly as possible from the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources in Ottawa to the several territorial administrations.
I should like to ask the minister if he has that suggestion in mind.
2. That the curricula used in northern schools be co-ordinated as closely as possible with those of the provinces immediately to the south of the several administrative districts.
I think that is a good suggestion and one which, if followed, would make sure that 28902-5-288J
Supply-Northern Affairs these children are getting a type of education similar to that received by the children to the south.
3.	That the northern adult education program be revised on more practical lines and administered within the several northern districts.
The commissioner goes on to make several recommendations as a result of what he terms the inefficiency of the department in dealing with this question.
In his fifth book-this was my second night of reading-the commissioner has this to say:
1.	The national parks be administered by a commission of members chosen from outside the public service, appointed for specific terms and remunerated for their services.
I am not suggesting I agree with that. But it is recommended because of the inefficiency the commissioner found in the administration of the national parks. He recommends:
2.	The national parks commission be organized on essentially departmental lines but under a board of full time commissioners appointed for fixed terms and removeable only for cause.
I do not say I agree with that, either. Nevertheless, the recommendation is made in an attempt to improve the present situation.
3.	The operation of the northern school system be transferred as rapidly as possible from the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources in Ottawa to the several territorial administrations.
I would agree with that. Then follows the recommendation:
4.	The responsibilities of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration relating to Indians in the north be transferred to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources.
I do not know the reason for that recommendation. But the commissioner goes on to make several recommendations, and this is because he is critical of the administration of the department in these fields.
Now we come to the national parks. What does the commissioner have to say about them? I have been interested in national parks. I happen to know the Revelstoke national park fairly well indeed, and I know a large number of people who live in Revelstoke. I have some questions on the order paper with respect to the administration of that park and I am looking forward to getting answers to those questions. I would say this to the minister: the administration of the Revelstoke national park requires his closest scrutiny. I have talked to a couple of dozen well known citizens of Revelstoke, not necessarily members of our party, who are highly critical of what they claim is very wasteful expenditure in the administration of the national park in Revelstoke. I will deal with that subject in greater detail when I have had a reply to the other questions I have raised. The commissioner has this to say as will be found on page 38 of volume 2 of the report:

Supply-Northern Affairs
An undue involvement of park managers in detailed problems on a day to day basis compounded by delegation to them of insufficient authority to make decisions on the spot.
These are the unsatisfactory conditions he found. I judge from what the minister said tonight that he intends to remedy this situation by providing reforms which are long overdue. They have been delayed for years because there were administrators in Ottawa who would not let the reins of power go to provide for decentralization.
The commissioner goes on to say:
Financial records showing expenditures for local services and facilities not used to establish the basis of charges to residents for utilities, garbage collection and other municipal-type services.
Finally, he calls attention to:
An illogical and inconsistent pattern of rentals for land used for residential and commercial purposes.
He recommends that-
A complete review of national park policy should be undertaken.
I think that is a good suggestion. There is a tendency to give in to certain interests which would like to exploit the natural resources of the parks, either for mining, or for lumbering, or for some other enterprise. I think we have to be very careful not to trespass on the beauty and natural wealth of our parks in this respect.
The recommendations read, in full, that-
1.	A review be made of national park policy and a comprehensive statement of future goals be incorporated in the relevant legislation.
2.	The national parks be administered by a commission with members chosen from outside the public service, appointed for specific terms and remunerated for their services.
I have brought these things forward as reflecting the opinions of the commissioner. I am not saying I agree with all of them. However, he has found examples of inefficiency and maladministration in certain branches of this department. I have also referred briefly to the recommendations of the committee in 1960. I believe this department requires a thorough investigation and review of its activities. I believe such a review should be undertaken by the committee on mines, forests and waters next session-I am not suggesting there is adequate time in which to do it this session. I do think we should have a thorough investigation into the activities of the department carried out in a constructive manner in an effort to support the minister in his campaign for reform, progress and improvement. Let us hear the officials of the department. Let us hear witnesses from organizations which are interested in the work of all the various branches of the department. I think z thorough review along these lines would
[Mr. Herridge.l
lay the foundation of information and knowledge which would enable the minister to develop policy and reorganize on lines to meet the needs of the present day.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it goes without saying that on this question of the Northwest Territories and as regards the estimates of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, there are several matters to discuss.
Today, I should like to bring up another point concerning the Department of Northern Affairs an National Resources and the Northwest Territories. It has to do with a whole section of the coast line-and I feel the debate on these estimates provides a good opportunity to deal with it-which surrounds the provinces of Quebec and which is hers by natural and constitutional rights.
If we take the maps published by the Canadian government and look at map No. 10, in the Canada Atlas, entitled "Bathymetry and Orography-Eastern Canada", we see among other things the whole area of Quebec, including new Quebec, James bay and Hudson bay.
In the middle of Hudson bay, there is an inscription in very small type that says: All islands in Hudson bay and James bay are included in the Northwest Territories. It is written in very small type and may seem unimportant; it is somewhat inconspicuous from a typographic point of view, but it implies all the same very important and far reaching consequences for the province of Quebec.
When the Canadian government in 1912, turned over this part of the Northwest Territories, that is new Quebec, to the province of Quebec, the protocol of this transfer provided that the jurisdiction of the province of Quebec-and this is where the transfer becomes important-over the new territories would extend as far as the high-water mark exclusively, that is up to the limit of James bay and Hudson bay.
It means, in practice, that the area washed by the tides, high and low, and you know that in that part of the country the tides are often several miles wide on the shores of Ungava bay and all along the new Quebec shore line, that all that land, between high and low tide, lies outside the jurisdiction of the province of Quebec.
It means, in practice, that the province of Quebec does not have the right to build a wharf or a quay along the coast line of the province, from the Ontario border to the north, without the authorization of the federal

government. Therefore the province of Quebec cannot have any outlet to the sea, any bridge or quay without Ottawa's authorization.
It means also that all the islands near the shore, even if they are only a few miles or a few hundred yards from the mainland, are considered thereby to be outside the province of Quebec.
In this respect, one might mention that a particularly serious case is to be found at Port Burwell, a post inhabited by 80 Eskimos and with no permanent white resident. Not so long ago, the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources set up there a co-operative cold storage warehouse with a capacity of several thousand pounds. That post is located on Killinek island, which is separated from the mainland and, therefore, from the territory of the province of Quebec, by the strait of Forbes, which is only two and a half miles wide.
As illogical as it may seem, that post, located on an island of the province of Quebec, comes under the Northwest Territories administration, eastern Arctic region, with headquarters at Frobisher, south of Baffin island, which is quite a distance away.
To show what absurd consequences those limits that were imposed may bring, even as far as law enforcement is concerned, let us take for instance the case of an Eskimo residing in the province of Quebec. Should he have committed an infraction or a crime punishable before the courts of that province, he could escape from the Quebec police simply by taking refuge on an island located a few hundred yards offshore. The province of Quebec would then have to apply to Ottawa for permission to pursue a person subject to arrest or the mounties from Frobisher or Cape Dorset would have to travel a very long distance to come and arrest that person and then hand him over to the Quebec authorities for prosecution.
We must not forget also-and that is another of the very important consequences of the present boundaries of these islands and frontiers between the Northwest Territories and the province of Quebec-that commercial, industrial and mining corporations wanting to evade the laws of Quebec in fiscal, labour or social matters, might establish themselves on the very shores of new Quebec, but below the limits at high tide; consequently, those industries would be located on the shores but on the other side of the point reached at high tide; those industries, although on the normal territory of the province of Quebec, but because the tide goes a little higher, would be located in the Northwest Territories.
Supply[DOT]-Northern Affairs
The same thing would happen if an industry or a plant were to locate on an island lying a few hundred yards from the province of Quebec, or even immediately adjacent to the shore. Then those establishments would be considered as part of the Northwest Territories and would not have to account to the province of Quebec for anything.
Those are obviously matters that must be put right to avoid Quebec being faced one day with precedents that might prove extremely dangerous to its territorial sovereignty.
That natural boundary, passing above the high water mark, as it is today, may moreover, result in a serious restriction of the rights of the province of Quebec in matters of toponymy. Indeed, the government of Quebec experienced some difficulties in this respect hardly a year and a half ago.
Actually, the government of Canada could refuse Quebec the right to name or change the names of any coast inlets: fjords, bays, creeks-as it happened indeed in late 1961, and, again, in February 1962-under the pretext that those geographical features are within the limits of the Northwest Territories.
I think, Mr. Chairman, it will be easily realized that the whole situation is really nonsensical, because the Canadian territorial waters limit off the Canadian coast is set at three miles. Consequently, the law should apply to the whole country, and also to each part of this country. At any rate, it should be pointed out that all the islands in the St. Lawrence and its estuary belong to Quebec, whatever their distance from the coast.
The foregoing remarks prove that it is absolutely essential to consider, with the briefest possible delay, the following rectification of the Quebec boundaries:
1.	Awarding to Quebec of the whole coast lying at low tide-and I repeat low tide- from the Ontario boundary, at the end of James bay, to the eastern entrance to the Hudson strait.
2.	Awarding to Quebec all islands within the territorial waters limit, according to the Canadian concept of that term, that is up to three miles off the limit at low tide, whereas today, the Northwest Territories extend to the limits at high tide.
We would like the whole boundary to be based on that three mile limit at low tide. Such a provision would imply among other things, that the province of Quebec take back the Button islands at the eastern entrance of Hudson strait, as well as the Diana Bay islands, the Digges islands, which are located immediately to the west of cape Iberville, at the western entrance of the Hudson strait, Smith island with Cap-d'Youville (cape Smith), the Jemmeraie or Hopewell islands,

Supply-Northern Affairs the isles of Nastapoka and Manitouc as well as Grande He (or Great island) on the Hudson bay coast.
3.	We should also consider the annexation of various islands situated off the territorial waters limits of Quebec, which appears particularly appropriate: Akpatok island in Ungava bay, Charles and Wales islands, in Hudson strait, Mansel island at the western entrance of Hudson strait, the Ottawa isles, the King George and Sleeper islands, the Bakers Dozen and the Belcher, all in Hudson bay, and finally, Charlton island and the Twin isles, in James bay.
Mr. Chairman, I submit that if you study the map of the Northwest Territories and of their islands, which surround the province of Quebec, you will readily admit that Quebec is entitled to consider these islands as part of its territory.
All these islands are situated directly in the normal zone of influence of the province of Quebec, just as the island of Anticosti and Hes-de-la-Madeleine, though situated much beyond Quebec territorial waters, are very much within the zone of economic and maritime influence of Quebec; that is why they fall quite naturally within the jurisdiction of that province.
Moreover, most of the islands I mentioned are made of calcareous or crystalline rocks, as is the case for Charles island or for the Belcher islands which are used as hunting grounds by the Eskimos of the various posts in new Quebec.
It must be said that as a general rule, those islands do not seem to contain very promising mineral resources, although some contain limestone which could be developed for construction purposes. By the way, the Eskimos use them and bring out some chips.
It must be mentioned also that in the Belcher islands, are found some iron ore deposits which are said to be quite interesting.
The annexation to the province of Quebec of all those islands with a surface larger than that of all the islands located in the St. Lawrence river and in its estuary is an imperative and urgent need in order to put a stop to the present territorial nonsense, and especially to see to it that the province of Quebec is not completely surrounded by all that series of islands later on, should another province be constituted out of that part of the Northwest Territories.
In any case, it would be illogical to annex those islands and archipelagos to any influence zone other than that of the province of Quebec.
This revision of the natural boundaries will permit, moreover, to establish the undisputable sovereignty of Quebec on Killinec
[Mr. Gregoire.l
island, where is situated the Port Burwell post, and also on the whole zone of the movement of the tides, which is, for Quebec, of capital importance.
Mr. Chairman, now that I have dealt to the best of my knowledge with this question of the boundaries of the province of Quebec and the surrounding islands, I would like to touch on another subject which is particularly close to our hearts.
When we look at the official maps of the province of Quebec, and even at those of the federal government-I have one which has been published by the "Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources", we may read:
The boundaries between Labrador and Quebec are not indicated, and for good reasons.
That is why those boundaries are not mentioned or marked on the geographic maps of the province of Quebec.
That simple note which appears on the maps of the province of Quebec sums up the whole problem of the boundaries between Quebec and Labrador.
In fact, the province of Quebec has never recognized, and rightly so, the principle of the decisions which were imposed by a judgment of the privy council, in London, in 1927, at the time of the trial that opposed Canada and Quebec to Newfoundland.
It is therefore the interpretation of the judgment and not the judgment itself which resulted in the fact that Canada and the province of Quebec never agreed on the new boundaries as they are shown in some instances.
In certain areas of that imposed boundary, the province of Quebec is facing an unbearable de facto situation.
According to reliable sources, it seems that mining concerns have assumed the right to draw the boundaries inside mining claims. Since those companies enjoy important material privileges in Newfoundland, such as lower royalties and provincial taxes, they have an obvious interest to settle on the so-called Newfoundland side and to push the boundary back to the Quebec territory, for the benefit of Newfoundland, and, of course, their own one.
They sort of play at see-saw, and they settle on the side where taxes are lower. This is prejudicial to both Newfoundland and the province of Quebec.
For instance., the Iron Ore company has installed at Labrador city, in the so-called Newfoundland territory an ore concentrator for which they pay operation taxes to Newfoundland.

Furthermore, Newfoundland demands that the majority of workers employed by that company, in that so-called Newfoundland territory, be Newfoundlanders.
Thus the province of Quebec is deprived of its due in many fields.
In view of such provocations, I am afraid that Quebec's empty protests are no longer sufficient because the mining companies are taking advantage of the Quebec government's present inaction.
Yet, the province of Quebec would have to make only one move to stop the shipment to Seven Islands, by railroad, of the iron which comes from the so-called Newfoundland territory. It would be so simple.
That is how, in our opinion, the question of boundaries should be settled.
The province of Quebec can obviously not remain idle in the presence of those facts.
We hope that action will be taken following the revealing statements concerning the frontiers of Labrador which were made by the Quebec minister of natural resources, Mr. Rene Levesque, when he made a tour of New Quebec, in July 1961.
This is how we disagree with the interpretation of the judgment which was handed down in 1927.

Mr. Chairman, in my opinion my remarks are in order, because this question has not yet been settled and does not come under any particular jurisdiction, except that it rests with the federal government to take a decision in that respect as soon as possible. Among all federal departments, I think that the matter comes under the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources and this is why I take this opportunity today to point out this matter to the house. I am asking the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Cantin) to let us deal with a problem which is so important for the province of Quebec and to which he should himself give more consideration.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I would like to explain a judgment delivered in 1927 and I will thus

Supply-Northern Affairs prove that my remarks are in order. Anyway,
I will not take more than three or tour minutes.
It will be recalled that the 1927 judgment essentially dealt with an interpretation of the term Labrador coast. This interpretation, Quebec has the right to reconsider it, because it is a real geographic aberration. The proof is that there is probably not a single geographer in the world who would apply to the word "coast" the description given by those who were responsible for the enforcement of the judgment.
In fact, on the strength of such an argument based on the interpretation of those who delivered the judgment, the coast of Brazil, through the Amazon basin, would extend to the Andes; the Mediterranean coast up to Ethiopia, through the White Nile and the Blue Nile; and the shores of the Black sea, through the Danube, would extend up to Austria, Hungary and even up to Switzerland, Germany and Czechoslovakia.
It is therefore because of such nonsense that the frontiers of the Newfoundland section of Labrador have been pushed back a distance of 450 miles or more within the province of Quebec, when they should have been set near the coast, as was recommended by representatives from Canada and Quebec.
A frontier established from the watershed is unacceptable to the province of Quebec; and it seems that the only reasonable and acceptable solution would consist in the determination or the setting of a frontier parallel to the coast, which would correspond, at a distance of from six to twelve miles within the mainland, to the outline of the present lay out, from the limits of the low waters on the coast, the low tide limits.
Thus, the unquestionable Newfoundland rights on the whole Labrador seashore would be fully respected and recognized. Such a solution would permit Newfoundland to maintain full and entire "jurisdiction"- which it exercises just the same nowadays- over the settlements at Forteau, Anse Eclair, Pointe Amour, Anse a Loup, St. Modeste, Carol Cove, on Simpson straits, St. Lewis Bay, Hawke Island, Cartwright Harbour, Northwest River, Goose Bay, Makkovic, Hopedale, Nain, Ford Harbour, Hebron and Saglec on the Atlantic Coast.
Such a solution would moreover represent a definite improvement over the proposal made by Canada in 1927, whereby Newfoundland was to be given a coastal belt of one mile only.
Mr. Chairman, I will conclude my remarks on Labrador by saying that because of the serious prejudices the present anomalies and lack of precision in the natural and political

frontiers of new Quebec represent for Quebec's sovereignty, the finding of an overall and final solution, consonant with the higher interests of the province in its new Quebec territory, has become an imperative and even an urgent matter.

In January of 1964, Canada's application will be placed before the Olympic committee at Innsbruck. Mr. Diefenbaker. I know, and I feel very keenly, the fact that laughs and jibes have been directed at the Canadian north, and northern development, not just by members of any one political party but by a great many southern Canadian- southern Canadians who neither know nor understand what it means to breathe fresh air, and who have forgotten how to pioneer,

Let me tell you, Mr. Chairman, by any yardstick you care to use, be it miles of road, school classrooms, hospital beds, welfare houses, nursing stations, or that great old yardstick, dollars, more was done in the Canadian Northwest Territories during the period 1958 to 1962 than in all the years from confederation onward put together. speechtext:
The hon. member for Toron-to-Rosedale insists on interrupting me tonight as he did the other night, but this will not prevent me from laying the record, concerning the Northwest Territories, before the committee. One development of special local, national and international significance occurred during this period. By virtue of the Nielsen bill the federal franchise was extended for the first time to the thousands of Canadian citizens living in the eastern and central Arctic, and in the Keewatin district of northern Canada.
It had local significance because this is the first time the Eskimo people had been consulted in any meaningful manner. It had national significance because it showed that the bill of rights was in fact a viable and dynamic document guaranteeing to every Canadian citizen the right to vote. It had international significance because it showed that in Canada at least, and at last, we were a country that understood that the ballot, the right to vote, is the foundation of democratic government.
I want to deal now with a phase of northern development that has just begun. I speak of the greatest resource which the northern territories have: their human resource. We must never be fooled into thinking that schools, hospitals and roads by themselves constitute the human development program. It is not enough for northern schools to produce graduates if the potential resources to provide jobs for those graduates lie dormant. It is not enough for our multi-million dollar hospitals in the north to repair diseased lungs if hunger and cold await the discharged patients from those hospitals. Surely the immediate task that faces the government in the Canadian north is to tie in a physical resource development program with its human resources, to stamp out the double curse of pov-
[Mr. Rheaume.l
erty and disease that still afflicts almost every non-white resident of the Canadian Northwest Territories.
Surely a country that has the courage, foresight and the money to build highways, railways and schools can now focus its energies on the shacks, tents and igloos that still exist in the Northwest Territories to blight the mind and heart of everyone who has the eyes to see them. Surely the government can now devote greater energy to providing jobs for all our northern people, not just for the swarms of graduates starting to come out of our northern schools but for the older people in the Northwest Territories who are now dependent on meagre welfare handouts when they cannot eke out a precarious existence in 55 degrees below zero weather.
I for one cannot feel happy when confronted, as I have been on numerous occasions in my travels throughout the Northwest Territories, with the anomaly of superheated, fresh-vegetable-filled D.E.W. line sites put there at fantastic cost to the Canadian government, in the very presence of our Eskimo people who spill their tattered and ragged lives digging in D.E.W. line garbage heaps, attempting to survive under the worst living conditions on earth.
I have had the opportunity to hold private conversations with the minister of northern affairs and with his parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George. I agree with the statement the minister made to the press in relation to housing. While he and I may not agree on many things, as has been obvious from my grievance, we do agree that there is no point in attempting to rehabilitate an Eskimo or an Indian who is cold, who is hungry or who is in rags. In the last five years in the Canadian Northwest Territories some 400 housing units were built for these people. I merely wish to say this: The job has just begun. On the basis of my conversations with the minister I am sure that neither he nor his parliamentary secretary will be happy until every person living in the Canadian north has a decent house and an opportunity to preserve the health and decency of his family. We will not be happy until we know that no Canadian citizen must attempt, in 1963 or in some future year, to chase scarce caribou in 55 degree below zero weather in the hope of finding something for himself and his family to eat.
The Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources has a large staff in the Northwest Territories as a result of a decentralizing process which began about three years ago. There are now field officers in many parts of the Canadian north, and the

minister, together with his parliamentary secretary, visited many of these men on his recent trip. I, for one, approve completely of the program whereby services in the remote parts of Canada were decentralized. I also wish to say that, with one or two startling exceptions, the staff of the department is excellent. I think the time has come when the minister, his deputy and his senior officers must see to it that these staff members are given greater authority. This is the only way in which they will be able to make their maximum contribution to the development of the Canadian north.
The myth is widespread in the Northwest Territories that the federal government has a monopoly on idiots. However, these officers are, for the most part, competent and dedicated men who are anxious to carry out programs which are in the best interests of the people of the north. They are capable of carrying out these programs. The reason they are capable of doing so is that, not only do they possess the qualifications which took them into a pioneer country, but they have the experience of living there. I myself lived for five years in the Canadian Arctic hundreds of miles from medical services. I know what it is to have children born two hundred miles north of the Arctic circle, with all the anxiety this places on an officer serving the crown and on the members of his family. I know that in many instances the competent and dedicated efforts of those officers who choose to go into the Canadian Arctic are hampered by a lack of authority. By this I mean that the staff of the department in the field must not be relegated to the role of message carriers. Too often this happens. I could give the committee an example. A field officer 200 miles north of the Arctic circle was not able, because of existing procedures, to approve a program whereby a young Eskimo girl could go to Edmonton to take a hairdressing course. The matter had to be referred to a committee composed of the heads of the department of northern affairs in Ottawa. It would have involved only $160 to settle this particular problem, yet the time alone of those senior officials who had to consider it was worth some $1,000. I will not take the time of the committee by giving further examples of this kind. I will merely say to the minister, now that he has decentralized responsibility in the Canadian north: For God's sake give these officers authority to act.
The Northern Canada Power Commission is also an agency for which the minister is responsible. I would ask that in his review of the department the hon. gentleman should take a close look at the cost of electricity to 28902-5-289J
Supply-Northern Affairs private consumers in the Canadian Northwest Territories. For the most part, those who use electricity in the north are civil servants or officers of the crown, and they do not pay directly for the cost of electrical services. But those people who are seeking to set up homes of their own and who are not employed by the crown, those who are seeking to establish businesses and develop the country, do have to pay their own bills. I do not exaggerate when I say that a typical light bill in the Northwest Territories for a private consumer will amount to over $100 a month for normal services. Somehow or other, the Northern Canada Power Commission must be convinced that, as a crown agency, it has a special responsibility to see to it that private citizens and private businessmen in the territories are not prevented from operating successfully or inhibited against entering the region because of the exorbitant cost of power.
I should like the minister in his dealings with the commission to consider the fact that in every Canadian northern community electrical services are provided only to those who are there as civil servants or as employees of the Hudson's Bay company, as members of the R.C.M.P. or of some other government agency. In every case when the commission installs a power plant in the territories, the people who benefit from the electricity and from all the things it can mean include everybody except the Indians and the Eskimos. I have asked questions about this, both of the minister and of the power commission and I am usually told: "The Indians did not ask for it"; or, "the Eskimos have failed to ask us for such a service."
Well, there are many things for which the Indians and the Eskimos in the Canadian Northwest Territories did not ask. But they got them. They got our Criminal Code. They got our regulations on trapping, hunting and fishing. They got our health standards which are now enforced. Surely, the Canadian government does not want to say that, until such time as the Indians and Eskimos come to them and fill out the necessary forms asking for electricity, electricity cannot be given to them. Surely, the time has passed when we should run a power line right over the roofs of the houses of the Indian and Eskimo people on its way to an R.C.M.P. station for example, without seeing that those people derive some share of its benefits? Surely if we can send our children in the north to million dollar schools-and I approve of this-we should not expect the same children to come home to study by coal oil or gasoline lamps if, indeed, they have such lamps. In many cases the only light available is candlelight.

Supply-Northern Affairs
I hope, indeed I am certain, that the minister will make a careful review of job opportunities for the Indians and the Eskimo people in the territories. For many years those of us who have worked in the department said to private enterprise: We have hundreds of Indians and Eskimos who are out of work; for goodness sake employ them in your projects. This has been going on for many years. The government of Canada has been the worst offender in the territories in making use of local labour, yet it is the major employer in the Northwest Territories.
We have made a promise to the Indian and Eskimo people of the north. Speaking on behalf of the people of Canada, we have said: Give up your children; give up your culture; give up your traditional methods of hunting, trapping and fishing; these things can no longer serve you; if you do, there is a new life for you. The minister of northern affairs must see to it that we do not let these people down after they have sent their children thousands of miles at six years of age to attend residential schools. Often they do not see their youngsters from one year to the next. They have done these things and, surely, we now have a special responsibility to see to it that the Eskimo and Indian children of the Northwest Territories who decide to throw in their lot, somehow or other with the people of southern Canada, are not betrayed in the trust they have shown. In this regard there have been some excellent examples of private enterprise and private industry in the Canadian north which have made extensive use of local labour. I think for example, of the Peter Bawden Drilling Company of Calgary, which went out of their way to make sure that, when they put down the first wildcat drill at Winter Harbour, on Melville island in the high Arctic, the men who operated the drill were Eskimos. I do not want to suggest for a second that Peter Bawden, who is a good friend of mine, does not know the value of a dollar; I merely want to suggest that he went out of his way to see to it, long before he commenced his operations, that Eskimo men were brought from the Canadian north, in co-operation with the department of northern affairs, trained in the work of a drilling rig, and taken back to carry out the job which he knew needed special men, men peculiarly adapted to the rather difficult climatic conditions of the Canadian north.
I think also of the Hudson's Bay Company; and believe you me, Mr. Chairman, there are many people in the Canadian north who would like to knock the Hudson's Bay Company. One thing about the Hudson's Bay Company-I have suggested this before in this house and I say it again-is that they
[Mr. Rheaume.l
made extensive use of local labour, the Eskimo and Indian people, in their operations in the Canadian north. They used them-and I use the verb in its best sense- extensively, to be sure that those people who were there had an opportunity to lead a decent life and receive a fair wage. I think of the mine at North Rankin inlet which made a point of using Eskimo labour when it opened up some 500 miles north of Churchill, a step which has now been followed by some of the mines in Yellowknife.
The Canadian government, which has the primary responsibility to see to it that this vast labour pool in the Canadian north is utilized, must start showing some leadership in this regard. It is not enough to go to a construction company and to say: "For goodness sakes hire Eskimo and Indian people", when at the same time the Canadian government, with its many departments-the Department of Transport, the Department of Justice, the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources and the Department of Public Works-is importing men from the Canadian south to fill jobs which too easily could be filled by Eskimos and Indians. You need look no further than the crown corporation, Northern Transportation Company, which this summer imported some 200 workers from the south, even for unskilled positions, to an Arctic community when there was a labour pool there of 120 Eskimo men trained in Arctic work, trained in navigation on the coast, and not one of them was hired.
I think it is time that before the Canadian government starts lecturing private businessmen in the north they had better set the pace themselves.
There are other areas of the Northwest Territories, Mr. Chairman, which I hope the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources will examine very carefully, with the whole of the government of Canada, through this department, carrying out func- _ tions which could better be carried out by private enterprise on the spot. I think, for example, of such things as the maintenance of the new Mackenzie highway to the Canadian north. Let me say that the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources now maintains several hundred miles of road into the Canadian north as a result of a decision made by the former government. The department of northern affairs owns the machinery and hires the staff to do it.
I also wish to go on record at this point as categorically saying that the decision to allow the government to do this in competition with the private companies which were able and willing to do it was a mistake. It was, I say categorically, a mistake. We should not allow the government of Canada to do this when

other private enterprise companies are there. That was one of the mistakes which I hope will not be repeated by the minister.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I want to assure the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources and his parliamentary secretary that they can count on full cooperation from both the hon. member for the Yukon and the hon. member for Northwest Territories, as well as all hon. members interested in the north, to help them convince other hon. members that the Canadian Northwest Territories is an area of special importance both now and in the future. More than anyone else, perhaps, I realize that the minister has many other responsibilities apart from the Canadian Northwest Territories. His department is a complex one. My great hope is that the door to the Canadian north will not be closed, and I am satisfied from my dealings with the minister that this will not be the case, that he has his main interest in the north, as had any other previous minister of the crown.
I have suggested, Mr. Chairman, that there are many other responsibilities which the minister of northern affairs has. One of these is the national museum, and knowing that the hon. member for New Westminster has a few things to say in this regard, at this point I will take my seat.

Unfortunately they have not taken in that very popular sport of the talking marathon. I commend the last speaker from the Northwest Territories for the sincerity of his appeal, although I was in a quandary at one stage when he told us that things were never so good as they were in the last five years in the Northwest Territories, and subsequently told us of the ravages and ills which exist in that unfortunate part of the country today. So I am not quite sure which was the case. But whichever it was-
