On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member quoted me as
Supply-Northern Affairs saying, on the one hand, that things were wonderful initially, and that subsequently they were terrible. If he had been listening he would have found out that I said a massive effort had been made in the Canadian north, but that we had just begun, that there were still many tasks facing the minister of northern affairs, and I said I hoped he would continue with the maddeningly slow job of raising the living standards of the Canadian north. I said that only a start had been made.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for clarifying that point. I would point out it would thus appear that, in spite of whatever efforts they may have made, the last administration did not succeed in rectifying the great problems which exist. I believe the department under the present administration will take giant steps in this direction and undoubtedly exceed any efforts made by the past administration.
In this regard I should like also to join the hon. member for Kootenay West in commending the minister on his appointment, and in wishing him well. I feel, as the hon. member for Kootenay West stated, that this department has a challenge facing it second to none. There may be other departments upon which the spotlight of today, in the economic crises of the present, is focused more brightly from day to day; but I think there is no department upon which the tomorrow of Canada, and the day after tomorrow of Canada, depends more than upon his department. I believe in this minister and in this department we have great hopes for our tomorrow.
I think it is a fair criticism that posterity will have to level at our generation and at those who came before us, and it is one of the tragedies of this nation, that undoubtedly over the years we have prostituted our national resources. We have used them for today as we saw fit. We have been spoiling them, eating them and generally using them up for today's purposes without any thought of tomorrow. In this regard I suggest that one thing which is needed very badly, and has been needed very badly in the past, which comes within the compass of this department, is a national conservation policy whereby there may be some planning in the use of our resources, so that there may be some direction as to the use of those resources, their preservation and rehabilitation, to the end that we may leave something of the great yesterday for those who come tomorrow. I think this applies not only to water resources but also to timber resources, wildlife and other natural resources. I hope the minister and the department will have the ability, the great courage and the perseverance which it

Supply-Northern Affairs will take to conceive such a national conservation policy, to bring it to fruition and to fight tooth and nail against the many vested interests that would undoubtedly oppose such a policy. This is something that has been very badly needed and I suggest that, irrespective of the hurrahs of today in the newspapers, the mark of history will be great for whatever minister of northern affairs and national resources has the political acumen, the foresight and the courage to bring in a truly important national conservation policy. I hope this will be done during the tenure of the present minister, and in the not too distant future under the present administration.
If I may move for a minute to the more parochial area of and adjacent to my own riding, I would point out that within 50 miles of the great capital of this country we have areas which are still undeveloped, great areas bordering the Ottawa river which might be used as a national bird sanctuary. In this land of ours we do not have too many such sanctuaries. It is possible that the United States has left us behind in this regard. I suggest it would be a great thing for Canada to have such a sanctuary within 40 or 50 miles of the capital. Right on the great Ottawa river, in the riding of the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue actually, there is a great undeveloped marshland where such a sanctuary could well be founded. I think it shows something of the impartiality of hon. members on this side of the house that I suggest that such a sanctuary be placed in the riding of the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue, because that part of the area is the best suited. If we were striving for industries I might not be so munificent, but I would be very pleased to let the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue have the ducks.
With regard to my own riding of Renfrew South may I suggest that in this very large riding there are great tracts of largely undeveloped land, land that has only been used to despoil it in some degree of its timber resources some generations ago, and which is now in the process of second growth. In this area there are great expanses of lakes which are as yet unopened because not even roads penetrate into some of these areas. These vast miles of undeveloped land are located some 75 to 100 miles from the capital of this country.
It is singular that we do not have a national park of stature in its pristine state, as the former minister said, within close proximity of the capital of the nation. I suggest to the minister that the lands in question are gradually being taken out of the public domain. They are being taken up for private use, and quite often by our friends and neighbours from the United States whom we are very

pleased to have there in the summertime as campers. Nevertheless, in this area within 75 to 100 miles of the city of Ottawa it will not be too long before the land is used for private purposes to such an extent that it would be too costly to bring it back into the public domain for use as a national park. Unless the department takes action within the next few years the opportunity will have been lost forever.
May I urge upon the minister that he consider this possibility. I know that in so doing he will consider all areas in close proximity to the city of Ottawa, but I think the principle of having a national park close to the capital city of Ottawa is surely something worth striving for at the present time. Certainly with the centennial of confederation approaching it would be a monument that would be well worth while. May I urge the minister to consider this matter. It is my submission that in considering it he will find no area so well suited as the large area of lakeland and wild and undeveloped land in the great riding of Renfrew South. If the minister will do this, I believe he will win a place for himself in the hearts of the people of Renfrew South and in the legend and history of that riding. If at the same time he brings forth a truly worth while, comprehensive, universal, national conservation policy he will also win for himself and his department a very great and enviable place in the history of Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am very sorry to note the lateness of the hour and to observe the shortness of the time left to speak on the subject of Canada's northern affairs and national resources. However, I should like to congratulate the minister on his appointment to this wonderful and important portfolio. I hope he will fill the appointment to the satisfaction of the people of Canada and will honour the position he now occupies.
Last summer I was very pleased to have the opportunity of meeting the new minister in Elk Island national park, which lies entirely within my constituency, on the occasion of the unveiling of the memorial to the pioneers of Ukrainian origin who settled in western Canada at the turn of the century. I might say that the people who were there at the unveiling were a little disappointed that the hon. member for Brandon-Souris, the former minister, was not there to unveil the memorial, because he was the one who authorized it to be placed in Elk Island national park.
I also want to say that the memorial is a memorial for people like Mr. Wasyl Eleniak who was the first Canadian settler from the Ukraine. He settled in the district close to Elk Island national park in 1891. He came

there some years after my people came to that district and the descendants of his family, his relations and the people he brought with him are my neighbours and friends today. He settled in what is now known as the Chipman area which is very close to Elk Island national park.
Up until about six years ago, I believe, Elk Island national park was the Cinderella park of Canada. It was originally started as a farm for the last herd of buffalo left in Canada after the great massacre of the 1880's. It was established as a reserve for the buffalo that were left. There are three phases to the operations of the park. It covers between 50 and 60 square miles and houses perhaps 500 buffalo. Many people in the area believe that the park should be able to provide plenty of food and pasture for 1,000 buffalo all the time. However, the wildlife experts think the number should be less.
This is one of the few parts that is comprised of the three phases. It has a wildlife phase, which embraces as I said about 1,000 buffalo, a great many moose, elk and deer; a recreation phase, composed of picnic areas, a swimming pool and other recreational facilities; and a farm where the food for the buffalo and other animals is raised so that they will not suffer in the wintertime. As I have said, many people around the area believe the basic herd should be approximately 1,000 instead of 500.
This park may seem like a local affair to some people, but it is not. There are approximately 200,000 visitors to this park each year and they come from every province in Canada as well as from the United States. As a matter of fact, they come from all over the world. It is truly, therefore, a national park. In addition to the recreational facilities which I mentioned, there is a nine hole golf course which is said to be one of the finest in the country. I would not know about that because I have never had a golf club in my hand. Some six years ago, as I said, this park was the Cinderella park of Canada. However, today there are two water purification plants, one for the use of the staff and one to serve the recreational area.
Since I do not wish to take up too much time of the committee, I want to say to the minister in conclusion that there are at least three things urgently required by this park. The first is a museum area. This area now contains only a replica of one of the original Ukrainian houses in our territory and a memorial to the Ukrainian pioneers. We wish that this museum area could be enlarged and a building erected that would house all the relics of the pioneers of western Canada. We also require a swimming pool, because at times the lake does not provide the best water
Supply-Northern Affairs for swimming. I have been told, too, that the recreational facilities would be improved with the addition of another nine hole golf course. If possible, it should be on a par with the one that is already there.
It may be that you think, as I said, this is a very local issue. It is not, because it concerns the people of Canada and the people who come from all countries to visit our national parks.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think it is a remarkable combination of history and geography that sees my friend, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, presiding over an empire of some 1,500,000 square miles in extent. This is an area roughly half the size of the continental United States. So far as I can understand from the Canada Year Book, the total population of that area could be placed in the Empire stadium in Vancouver for one of the larger football games. This disparity and lack of population probably only adds to the problems the minister has. This northern half of the nation is pretty well under an administration form of rule, and the problem of administering this great area rests on the shoulders of the minister and his administrative officers.
I think it is a fair comparison to say that the minister is responsible for problems in an area about the same of, or rather larger in extent than that which is operated at the present time by Mr. Ben Bella, who is running an area called Algeria. This vast territory includes the Yukon, Northwest Territories and national parks. As you know, the national parks themselves occupy an area larger than several of the states of Europe. This department extends its activities and interests from the drilling of oil in the Arctic to luring tourists from San Francisco. It includes in its operations many museums. It has no less than 40,000 square miles of bird sanctuaries, an area especially for the birds. This department, with its responsibilities, its spheres of interest, has come to us as a sort of catch-all or northern upstairs attic in which a vast accumulation of things has been stored, or perhaps left in corners over the years. In our opinion in this party, this situation has prevailed for too long. It should be changed. We think the time is now for us to take, as a nation, a new look at the department of northern affairs and to bring under a more realistic arrangement some of its functions and responsibilities.
I would say, Mr. Chairman, that we should put it this way. We should go up in the attic of the northern affairs department to see what we have there after all these years, and certainly bring down what we can handle to better advantage or put in a better place. In a brief talk on this immense subject, one can

Supply-Northern Affairs do no more than to pick up, let us say, one small trunk out of the attic of northern affairs.
It seems surprising to me, and to many other Canadians, that this large department of northern affairs still has over-all responsibility for the national museum of Canada. Surely, with all its other officers and responsibilities, the department should be freed of the responsibility it has for the museum of Canada, the natural history branch and the human history branch. We say that these facilities should be made a separate entity. We think that they should be placed in the same category as the national film board and the national gallery, under a separate authority of their own. In time I hope to see developed in Canada what might well be called a national ministry of culture, which would bear responsibility for all these cultural activities.
I think that part of the dissatisfaction and trouble through which the national museum has gone, and is still going, has emanated from the fact it remains as a sort of leaf on the end of a branch on the end of a tree. In my view, it should be re-examined, strengthened and given a new foundation. It should have more scope to develop its own policies and resources. There is no use, Mr. Chairman, belabouring the present minister or the former minister of this department for the reported unhappy conditions in the national museum of Canada. Neither of them had the time or, I think, the energy to do all the other things they had to do and at the same time take up and solve the problems of the national museum to put it on a modern footing in 1963.
It is not my intention to belabour the unfortunate museum tonight any more than I can help. However, it will be fresh in the minds of many members that earlier this year, less than two months ago I believe, four prominent officials of the museum resigned. They were Dr. Russell, director of the natural history branch; Dr. McFeat, chief ethnologist; Dr. Larry Oschinsky, physical anthropologist, and Dr. MacNeish, chief archaeologist. When the government was asked why this happened they said, in effect, that it was too bad.
There was no connection between these resignations taking place at roughly the same time; it was sort of a coincidence. Perhaps these men had better jobs to which to go. This is hard to credit, particularly when I am told that over the last two years there have been no less than 30 resignations from the museum staff. I feel it is obvious there is a lack in the national museum of Canada in its present relationship to the northern affairs

department. There should be scope for leadership. It is hindered by being kept tied to the apron strings of the department. It should be given new foundations, and its functions should be expanded and extended so that it can play a much more realistic part in our Canadian culture.
In conclusion I would ask that the minister and the government consider, first, taking the museum out of its present outmoded context as a corner in the department of northern affairs; second, that they make it a separate branch or entity, such as the national film board and, third, I would ask that they consider appointing a director general for the national museum system of Canada which we hope to see evolved in the future.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to make a few remarks here on the basis of what had been under consideration in the department, under the previous administration. It may be that what I have to say might have been taken up privately with the minister, but after listening to the hon. member for Renfrew South I think I too should have the opportunity of stating my case for the area in which I live. Some time ago I had the privilege of putting a case forward for the extension of the small park that exists north of the Bruce peninsula at Georgian bay. This is a natural area for the extension of a park site, and includes Flower Pot island off the northeastern tip of the peninsula.
I listened to the minister saying how valuable our national parks were, and how our people, and many thousands from the United States, spend their vacations on the highways rather than going to specific sites, as was the custom previously. He told how they spend so much time on the roads travelling from one point to another, and this was exactly why I made my presentation to the department some time ago, and convinced the minister of that day that consideration should be given to this development.
I have before me a proposal for a national park on Bruce peninsula in the province of Ontario. Ontario does not have much of this type of institution, and this I believe is because of the farsighted programs of the provincial authorities. These programs are to their credit, but I believe that the provision of a national park would be valuable in this particular area.
We sometimes speak of the natural things we lose as the result of commercialization of an area. We speak of the loss to the country

of certain types of growth, of certain aspects of natural beauty lost through commercialization. There are specific types of flora and fauna on the Bruce peninsula which will disappear in the not too distant future, if the investigation that was carried on with regard to a national park is not continued.
I also have a letter before me which I received earlier this year when I discussed the situation with one of the residents of that area. They are extremely enthused and interested in the project. I might add, Mr. Chairman, that this is not in my constituency, and therefore I feel I have the right to be very frank about my presentation. I have here an outline of all those things which would be of advantage to Canada, and in particular to the advantage of Canadians who visit that part of the country.
I agree with the minister when he says there is a trend on the part of vacationers to travel from site to site, using parks facilities and that sort of thing. Within about 90 or 100 miles of this area there are other provincial parks, and I believe this area would be an ideal link in the chain of great lakes parks. It would be valuable not only for highway travellers but for those who use the waters of the great lakes, and at present tremendous numbers of Americans enter Canadian waters at Georgian bay.
I think I can impose upon the good will and honesty of the minister to follow this up in the vein in which it was first thought of and presented. I hope he will allow me to discuss it on a personal basis with him in an effort to further this worthy project on the tip of the Bruce peninsula.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was going to say a word on the general item, and pay numerous compliments to the minister, but that would be now out of order. I appreciate his comments about the use of the parks, and his rather gracious tribute to the prosperity which the country has enjoyed for the last six years, as indicated in the use of our national parks by the motor owning public.
Specifically I would like to direct his attention to the park in Prince Edward Island which, as his figures show, has the second highest attendance of all. I may say I have often quarrelled with the figures of his department, because they do a little process of cooking them with regard to a lot of people who go into the park several times a day. I know that when I entered Banff I was counted as a visitor, whereas I was going to British Columbia and should not have been called a visitor. Perhaps I will have to carry on the argument I had with the former minister, the hon. member for Brandon-Souris about the figures which the department uses-and I may
Supply-Northern Affairs add that the former minister was one of the best ministers in the government I supported. A certain part of Canada has been described as the land God had given to Cain, but I would like to quote Jacques Cartier, the first tourist to Prince Edward Island who in 1534 described it as:
-the fairest land that might possibly be seen... full of beautiful trees and plains.
There is a fine national park in this area. It is very important to our economy, to our burgeoning and expanding tourist industry, and I would urge the minister most strongly to appoint a permanent superintendent for it. We have had two acting superintendents there since the departure of Mr. Kipping, who was one of the most outstanding men in the national parks field. To indicate the type of man Mr. Kipping was, he was a born Cape Bretoner, who became a Prince Edward Islander, and it is a man with judgment and experience like that whom we would like to have as superintendent of the park.
I mention this to the minister at this time, because next year is centennial year in Prince Edward Island, and I am sure the figures for attendance at the park will be greater than ever before. In my opinion it is of the utmost urgency that he do not revert to the earlier practice of having acting superintendents, but that he appoint a full time man to knuckle down to the important job of developing this park.
I would also like to say we are hopeful for a little more rapid development of the site at Fort Amherst, with which so much of our history is bound up, both of the French occupation and the English occupation. I would also commend to the minister a most careful study of the suggestions which have come from the provincial government regarding recreational areas in the provinces. A very pleasing thing about national parks attendance is that more of the native peoples are making use of these beautiful areas, and we also find this in Prince Edward Island. It is for these reasons I urge him to do these two things. I think the minister has, indeed, started out to be what one might call a good minister. I will make no comparisons with anyone else. I do wish him well and I hope he will earn a place of esteem and regard in his ministry comparable to that of the hon. member for Brandon-Souris.

speechtext:
Before we leave the question of parks, I should like to ask the minister about the prospects of developing Garibaldi park. There has been tremendous interest in the lower mainland of British Columbia in the possibility of developing that park. As the minister knows, there is a lack of park facilities in that area of the province. This

Supply-Northern Affairs park comprises one of the most beautiful locations in Canada. I know the minister is interested in this and I believe he has made statements publicly regarding his willingness to undertake such a project if he could reach an understanding with the government of British Columbia. I think it would be helpful to the committee to have something on record as to what the minister is prepared to do, what offer he has made, and what response he has received from the government of British Columbia.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I think I would be on happier ground talking about the Bruce peninsula park or about the Prince Edward Island park, which I have not seen, than I would be talking about the Garibaldi park. The so-called offer was, in fact, the renewal of an offer made by the Hon. Mr. Lesage when he was in charge of the department, and renewed, in 1958 I think, by my immediate predecessor, I think there is wide agreement that, of all the areas of Canada, both for summer and winter recreation, Garibaldi park is the outstanding place. I have talked with people who are very conversant with Europe and they say the Alps in no way compare with Garibaldi park. All I did was to renew the offer made by my predecessor suggesting that if the area were turned over by the province to the federal government, free of all encumbrances, as the National Parks Act requires, the federal government would develop it as a national park.
I am sure most hon. members would agree we do need development there. Instead of a great stream of tourists coming up from the south, pausing briefly at Vancouver and then going on to Banff and the other national parks, they would be retained for a time in British Columbia and would unquestionably spend more money there. We would also get back a great deal of money spent by our own people each winter in Washington on skiing.
I have hopes, though they may be growing fainter day by day, that the premier of our province will change his mind and decide to turn this great area over to the national government for development. I am certain it would be in the interests of our economy in British Columbia to do so. We are at the present time developing intermediate parks along the Pacific west of Jasper and Banff in order to hold some of the traffic which now is determined to get into the national parks, overcrowding them, requiring tenting facilities, and so on.
I should like to commend the hon. member for Grey-Bruce and the hon. member for Queens on the comments they have made. They have spoken of a common desire on

the part of Canadians, a growing desire, I think, in the light of the fact that we are approaching the centenary of our confederation, that we should set aside amply and in good time those remaining great areas which may be required in the next 50 years as national parks. I am certain that in parts of Ontario today, when people look back, they are sorry a greater provision was not made for the spaces which today are required by our people and which are, also, a great magnet for visitors from abroad.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: When the offer was made to the province of British Columbia to develop Garibaldi park, was an estimate made as to what the cost would be and how much the federal government was prepared to spend on the development of that area?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The government's attitude has been that when an area is turned over free of encumbrances by the province, an inspection is made. The area is laid out then according to the best views of our planners, and anything that is required to make a job of it is done. In Fundy park, New Brunswick, which is a relatively small park, we expended something of the order of $8.5 million. The principal requirement in many of these places is roads, and where large areas of rock are encountered this can be an expensive item. Our total capital expenditure in all the parks is of the order of $200 million. I did ask the premier of the province if he would agree to letting our planning officials into the area to suggest what might be done with it. I have a letter from him agreeing to that proposal, with the condition that the resources by way of minerals and timber would be retained as the property of the provincial government and be subject to its exploitation. This, of course, is a condition which makes it impossible for us to establish the area as a national park.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I will be as concise as possible. Tomorrow, we will continue with our consideration of the Income Tax Act, committee stage and third reading. Then we will take the resolution relating to the consumer credit committee; and if that is finished in time we shall take up the bills relating to the Northwest Territories. In the evening we will consider the estimates of the Department of Labour backed by those of the Department of Fisheries.
